#10232. ‘No one asked for this’: AI is being pushed on people—and they’re sick of it

The AI era is fully here—and while companies bill it as a solution to problems, consequences like mass layoffs, environmental effects, privacy concerns, and the slopification of culture have many people fed up with something they never wanted in the first place.

The technology faces growing resentment from workers, who are being urged to embrace AI tools even as businesses have rushed to reduce their workforces in favor of automation. 

Online, many posts about AI capture a growing frustration with how these tools—and their disruptions—are being forced on users.

“Nobody asked for Google to be worse—but AI made it happen,” one X user recently remarked. “No one asked for computer hardware costs to rise—but AI made it happen. No one asked for human customer service to be replaced—but AI made it happen.”

In another post, Sarah Hoyt, a science fiction, fantasy, and mystery author, said she doesn’t hate artificial intelligence, but is “begging all the crazy people out there to stop pushing AI where no one asked for it.”

The disenchantment plays out in the data: In 2019, 81% of Glassdoor reviews mentioning AI were positive, the company said, compared with 43% this year. Meanwhile, Pew Research found that 52% of Americans were more concerned than excited about AI, up from 37% in 2021. And in an Ipsos poll from June, 67% of respondents thought AI would worsen the worker experience.

“The closest analog is the replacement of physical labor throughout the long Industrial Revolution,” said Jiemin Tina Wei, an assistant professor of history at Florida International University. But in this case, it’s “brain work,” rather than manual labor, that’s being replaced. 

“And now, the industries that are getting allegedly wiped out are the ‘low-hanging fruit’ of white-collar work,” she said.

But gutted livelihoods aren’t the only reason many are anti-AI.

The productivity paradox

Louis Hyman, a historian at Johns Hopkins University who specializes in labor and the American economy, points to a “productivity paradox”: a contradiction that was also generally true of the rise of computers in the ’80s, in which similarly dizzying investments didn’t necessarily make people better at their jobs as promised.

He points to snags like the frequency of software updates. “Every time you learn how to do something, suddenly they break it, and you have to relearn it.” With the introduction of AI, it’s “as if all software is being updated, all at once, everywhere.” Another part of the equation, he said, is that it isn’t clear how some people are using AI tools.

Hyman said he uses AI to write software and automate “boring tasks”—for example, he wrote a script to rotate the thousands of photos he takes of historical documents during archive visits so they all face right-side-up. But, he said, “most people are not wanting to sit down and write Python code to automate their job. They just want to do their job.” 

Added to that is the deep fear of being replaced once the work is automated. “I’m a tenured professor—I literally can’t be fired,” he said. “If I automate some boring part of my job, that just means I have more time to do the more interesting parts of my job. And that’s not true for all people, right?” 

A new occupational hazard

Another reason many people push back on AI is the lack of adequate guardrails—especially when it could cause major issues at work.

In one case, an AI tool deleted a software company’s entire database. In another, AI was blamed for deleting a fully edited season of a Swedish reality show mere weeks before the scheduled premiere. In medical settings, AI scribes have put inaccurate information in patient records, raising the question of who would be held liable for resulting medical errors. 

Meanwhile, misreads by AI identification tools used by law enforcement have led to wrongful arrests and injuries, per the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) AI Risk Initiative. Other AI-generated errors have popped up in court documents, federal reports, news stories, and fast-food drive-throughs. 

“The main point I’ve pushed and will continue to push [regarding] AI is ‘no one asked for this,’” radio host Adam Xii said on X, in response to news that Anthropic hallucinated details in its defense during a music copyright lawsuit. “So when a product or service no one asked for suddenly becomes ubiquitous, one must ask: why? Because AI tools are meant to generate more wealth for the wealthy at the expense of creatives.”

At the least, AI’s convenience is being offset by a need to check its work that has created new opportunities for human error. The proliferation of “workslop” even led a tech company’s CEO to fully ban AI use, as Inc. reported this summer. 

“A lot of what I’ve seen is kind of annoyance at the proselytizers at work—or the people who are heavy adopters—creating a lot of extra work for the people around them,” because those people downstream then have to check the work, Wei said.

Wei added that content moderation and data annotation work “can be extremely mentally taxing.” Research has found that “good” challenging work will be both difficult and interesting to certain extents, she said. But checking output is both difficult—because you have to look for every small potential error—and boring.

“You’re not producing knowledge, but merely supervising the production of words, knowledge, content,” Wei said.

The unwanted technological advances continue

AI’s intrusive nature—accompanied, again, by the threat of replacement—is reflected in workers’ behavior, not just in fed-up tweetstorms. One report found that nearly a third of workers surveyed, and 44% among Gen Z, had tried to sabotage their companies’ AI strategies.

Section, an AI planning and upskilling company, recently reported that 69% of workers surveyed said their organization had encouraged the use of AI agents, but only 16% actually used them. And 38% said they use other AI features.

The frustration hasn’t seemed to deter tech companies.

“We heard you wanted Copilot Mode at work,” read an X post from Microsoft that promoted Edge’s Copilot Mode for Business.

“No, you heard wrong,” a computer technician replied. “Literally no one asked for all this AI. In fact, everyone wants to know how to remove it.” 

Questions of organizations

In some cases, it seems companies are starting to discover that automation has some shortcomings.

In the U.S., 32% of hiring managers who eliminated positions in favor of AI have had to reinstate the same or similar roles, according to research from consulting firm Robert Half. Similarly, Gartner predicts that by 2027, half of companies that attributed reductions in staff to AI will rehire people to perform similar work.

Wei said the mismatch between the hopes for AI and the reality of its adoption relates to a quote from Bill Haywood, a famous labor organizer, who said that “the manager’s brains are under the workman’s cap.”

In other words, Wei said, “It’s really ultimately the workers who possess the knowledge and the know-how to run day-to-day operations. Some people have argued that the history of labor is just managers trying to take back that knowledge in an attempt to replace workers in the production.

“And I guess some people experience AI that way—that it’s being [imposed] upon them so that they train, ultimately, their final, automated replacement.”

Hyman said that a better alternative to the “adapt or die” mentality would be for organizations to use the technology to empower their employees. They should “actually say, ‘okay, we’re gonna create organizational conditions that let you replace yourself, and then focus on the work that needs to be done’—because the amount of work to be done is not finite, right?”

“I get told on a nearly weekly basis that historians are going to be replaced,” Hyman said. “So, yeah, it depends on how valuable you think getting reliable information and history is.”

He added that a world “where the only source of history or journalism is from either Open AI or Anthropic” would feel like an “Orwellian nightmare.”

“That seems not a great road to go down,” he said.

#10231. How to Migrate an Elementor Site to the WordPress Block Editor

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Elementor made your site easy to build. It may also be making it slow. Here's how to move a site onto the Block Editor without breaking URLs, losing content or dropping out of Google.

Page builders solved a real problem. Before the Block Editor matured, they were the easiest way to give clients drag-and-drop layouts. Many of those sites are still running today, and a lot of them are slow on phones.

The data backs that up. According to the HTTP Archive Core Web Vitals Technology Report for June 2026, 36.8% of Elementor sites pass Core Web Vitals on mobile. Sites built with the Block Editor pass 53.0% of the time. That's correlation, not proof, since hosting and setup matter too. But in my experience, it matches what happens when you remove the builder from a slow site.

My reason for migrating sites off Elementor is simple: **page builders make websites heavy. **Having said that, Elementor has improved a lot. Its performance settings, Flexbox Containers, and asset-loading options cut much of the bloat, and a carefully tuned Elementor site can pass Core Web Vitals. But tuning only goes so far. You’re still shipping the builder’s framework, wrapper markup and scripts, and every plugin or Elementor update is a chance for the speed to slip again.

For small business sites that don’t need drag-and-drop editing, rebuilding the same design on the WordPress Block Editor (Gutenberg) removes that weight at the source, without changing what the client sees.

This guide follows the order I use. It assumes you're comfortable with WordPress admin, WP-CLI and a staging site. If you need to set those up first, SitePoint's guide to the ultimate WordPress development environment covers the tooling.

Not every Elementor site needs to move. Migration makes sense when:

It's harder to justify when the site leans on Elementor Pro features you'd need to replace, such as complex popups, dynamic loops or WooCommerce templates. Those can all be rebuilt, but the job gets bigger fast.

You can't prove a migration worked without "before" numbers. Capture these on the live site first.

Crawl the site with a tool such as Screaming Frog, and export every indexable URL with its title, meta description, H1 and canonical tag. You can also pull published pages and posts with WP-CLI:

Run Google PageSpeed Insights, which uses Lighthouse for its lab scores, on the homepage and two or three key templates. Save the mobile lab scores and, if the site has enough traffic, the field data from real users.

Export the last three months of pages and queries from Google Search Console. That's what you'll compare against after launch.

Elementor stores each page's layout as JSON in the elementordata post meta field, and marks builder pages with elementoredit_mode. This command lists every page that uses the builder:

Then list everything else Elementor controls, which is easy to miss:

On the small business sites I've migrated, the inventory usually turns up more than the owner expects. The pages are the easy part. The surprises are saved templates nobody remembers creating, a popup still running on every page, add-on widgets from plugins that were installed once and forgotten, and contact forms that live inside Elementor Pro rather than a form plugin. Finding those before the rebuild saves a broken launch.

Work on a staging copy. Install a block theme, such as Twenty Twenty-Five or a lightweight starter theme, and move the Elementor global styles into theme.json. That way colors, fonts and spacing are defined once, instead of in every widget.

Copy the hex values and font names from Elementor's Site Settings so the new site matches the old one. Rebuild the header and footer as template parts in the Site Editor. If you'd rather write a theme yourself, SitePoint's series on building a WordPress theme from scratch covers the basics.

Most Elementor sites repeat the same few sections: a hero, a services grid, testimonials and a call to action. Build each one once as a block pattern, then reuse it on every page. Patterns are plain block markup, so you don't need React to write them, whatever you may have heard about React and WordPress development.

In a block theme, any PHP file in the /patterns folder with a header comment is registered automatically:

For page content, there's a useful shortcut. Elementor saves a plain HTML copy of each page into post_content. Open a page in the Block Editor, and the old content usually appears in a Classic block. Choose Convert to blocks, then delete the leftovers and rebuild the layout with your patterns. It keeps the copy and images, so you only redo the design.

The difference shows up in the page source. Here's typical front-end markup for a single heading on an Elementor page, using the older section and column layout:

Newer Elementor versions with Flexbox containers and the optimized markup settings trim some of those wrappers, but most older sites still carry all of them. Multiply that by every element on every page, and the weight adds up.

To speed up this step, I built a free Elementor to Gutenberg converter. Paste in a page's elementordata JSON from Step 2, and it returns block markup you can paste into the Block Editor's code editor. It handles headings, text, images, buttons, spacers, dividers and column layouts, and lists anything it can't convert, such as forms and popups, for you to rebuild by hand. It runs entirely in your browser, so the page data never leaves your computer.

The code is rarely what holds a migration up. Content is. Once clients see their site being rebuilt, many decide it's time to rewrite their pages too, and the project ends up waiting on copywriters and approvals. My fix is to separate the two: migrate the existing content as it is, launch, then update the copy afterwards. That keeps the speed and SEO gains on schedule, and it means any ranking change can be traced to either the migration or the new copy, not both at once.

This is the step that decides whether rankings hold.

To spot-check a redirect or a status code from the command line:

When staging matches the live site, deploy it. Then:

Leave the old elementordata meta in place for a few weeks, in case you need to roll back. Once you're confident, take a backup and remove it to shrink the database.

Run PageSpeed Insights again straight away for lab scores. Field data takes longer: the Chrome UX Report uses a rolling 28-day window, so give it a month before judging real-user results. Compare Search Console clicks for the same period before and after launch.

In my migrations, the biggest change is usually page weight and loading time, because the builder's CSS, JavaScript and wrapper markup are gone. What doesn't always improve is server response time. If the site is on slow shared hosting, the first byte still arrives late, and that needs a hosting fix, not a rebuild. Search traffic should hold steady if the URLs and metadata were protected. If it drops, the Step 5 crawl comparison is the first place to look.

Moving off Elementor isn't a one-click job, but it isn't a full redesign either. Record a baseline, inventory what the builder controls, rebuild with patterns, and protect every URL. Most of the speed gain comes from removing code the site never needed. For what to tackle after that, see these practical web performance techniques. Most of the risk comes from rushing the SEO checks. Done carefully, the client gets the same site, a faster one, and an editor that comes with WordPress itself.

#10228. Why 2 Pinterest vets and a neurosurgeon are building a Reddit for doctors

Medicine’s complexity and ever-evolving nature means doctors will always have more to learn and discuss—but in the digital age, there’s also a question of where those conversations can best take place.

Online, healthcare workers’ discourse is distributed across various social media platforms, forums, and group chats. Meanwhile, offline, medical professionals are “hyper-specialized,” with limited opportunities to work with colleagues from other disciplines, according to Dr. Rohan Ramakrishna, chief of neurosurgery at New York-Presbyterian Brooklyn Methodist Hospital.

As a neurosurgeon who specializes in brain tumors, he said, “the doctors I interact with on a regular basis are radiation oncologists and neuro-oncologists, and that’s it.” Even hospital doctors’ lounges are disappearing, he added, removing another opportunity for doctors to socialize and discuss medicine.

So Ramakrishna teamed up with Vikram Bhaskaran and Arun Ranganathan—two Pinterest alums who previously led engineering teams related to creators, content, and partners—to cofound an app that could foster that sense of community. 

Initially, the trio envisioned Roon as a place for doctors to provide patients with information; but in the app’s early days, Bhaskaran said, they found that physicians were especially interested in seeing what their own peers had to say—so they decided to rework the platform to facilitate those interactions.

Now, a year after its launch, the platform is adding features that bring Pinterest’s focus on sharing to the thousands of physicians on the platform to share everything from treatment advice to conference photos. As social media apps shift and online misinformation proliferates, the founders are hoping Roon will help physicians separate the signal from the noise.

Where doctors gather online

In some ways, Roon’s concept echoes that of #MedTwitter, which became a widely used, informal hub for medical experts and others to exchange information, ideas, and opinions, creating “a completely open-source environment that democratizes medical information,” as two physicians wrote in 2021. The hashtag still exists, and some continue to use it, but Twitter’s transition into X—and the accompanying changes—scattered some of  #MedTwitter to other platforms.

But medical science is always evolving, Ramakrishna said, as are politics and policy changes, and doctors lack a “home” for making sense of it all. Roon is “a place where you have net new knowledge creation, because people are trying to unpack what it all means, and understand it together.” 

To help shape Roon’s knowledge-creation network, the company enlisted more than 400 “founding physicians” from a range of specialties and institutions, who the company said “are owners with equity in Roon.” 

“A year ago, we had kind of a thesis: that physicians should have a place online where they can collaborate, connect, and that was safe and private,” said Bhaskaran, and it’s “been really heartening” to see how physicians are now using Roon. 

Creating community for a core audience

Roon joins a growing number of communications platforms designed for clinicians. Doximity, a networking service that offers an AI scribe and other tools, says more than 85% of U.S. physicians are registered members. There’s also Sermo, Figure 1, Mednet, Doquity—which is used by clinicians across much of Asia—and other new ventures like Marit Health, where medical professionals can share salary data. 

Each of them varies in form and function. Roon, which has the benefit of being designed by Pinterest veterans, is built to look and feel like mainstream social media sites. On it, users discuss new research, policy changes, and health topics that emerge in the news cycle, Ramakrishna said, and ask for advice on patient care. For example, he said, a family medicine doctor who posed a question related to reproductive health and the pituitary gland got replies from peers in family medicine, OB-GYN, high-risk maternal-fetal medicine, neurosurgery and neurology. 

There’s also an ability to form private groups—for example, Ramakrishna said, there’s one for chief medical officers, and another for residential program directors—and a new, Pinterest-board-inspired “Collections” feature that lets users group related content and media together. 

Selective, intentionally

Roon also differs from most medical communications apps in that, for the time being, it’s exclusive to physicians—M.D.s and D.O.s—who are licensed in the U.S.

Bhaskaran says the criteria mean that Roon can function as a place to share expertise built in the field—something that augments published literature in an important way. 

“There’s so much of medicine that’s outside of the published literature, that’s not accessible via chatbot or via AI: that’s in people’s heads,” he says. 

Roon currently has tens of thousands of users, Bhaskaran says, noting the goal is to reach 250,000 by the end of next year. That would constitute almost a quarter of the 1.08 million physicians that were licensed in the U.S. as of 2024. 

Part of the challenge of growing is the fragmentation of physicians across various social media apps. Some physicians also say they value the diverse perspectives offered by other healthcare workers, like nurses and pharmacists, and by those in other countries. 

They do plan to invite certain non-physician specialties, like infectious disease scientists, Bhaskaran added, but they still have work to do to build up the community of physicians, which remains their first goal. They also plan to expand Roon internationally, “but again, very thoughtfully, because verification is just a little bit of a hard problem once you leave the United States.” In the meantime, the company has a waitlist for medical professionals who’d like to join.

Human amid AI

Roon currently employs AI for tasks like filling out physicians’ profiles, routing users’ questions to specialists, and generating summaries of content. Its team is also working on new AI-powered functions to keep users up-to-date, like an audio digest feature that summarizes medical news and related Roon posts.

Then, there’s the training question: a database of medical information based on real-life expertise would be valuable for training LLMs, and physicians on X have expressed concern about it being used that way. A company spokesperson said Roon “currently has no plans to sell its data,” though the company may use it to refine its own models, and hasn’t made a “definitive commitment ruling out all future uses involving third-party LLMs.” 

But in the face of AI’s all-consuming nature, “our thesis is actually [that] the human network will become more valuable over time, especially as most of the world goes, ‘hey, we’re unclear who wrote this content,’ or ‘everything you see on the internet is AI slop,'” Bhaskaran says. ”We’re taking kind of an old school bet—which is, there’ll be value for community, and that’ll transcend any specific technology.”

#10226. CMA Awards 2026: How to watch the 60th anniversary event and celebrate all things country music

Grab your best rhinestoned cowboy hats and boots—it is time for the Country Music Association Awards.

Much like the hairstyles in Texas, this year is going to be big, celebrating 60 years of the CMA Awards. From a Dolly Parton tribute to Brooks & Dunn’s special award to the Taylor Swift of it all, there is a little something for everyone live from Nashville’s Bridgestone Arena.

Let’s see what all the yee-hawing is about.

Who is nominated for a CMA Award?

Speaking of the Lone Star State, Ella Langley’s hit “Choosin’ Texas” is one of the singles that helped her score nine CMA Award nominations, the most of anyone this year.

Miranda Lambert is nominated seven times. Ben West and Kacey Musgraves will go into the evening with five nominations each.

Greenhorns Avery Anna, Carter Faith, Emily Ann Roberts, Tucker Wetmore, and Stephen Wilson Jr. are all nominated for New Artist of the Year.

Fan favorites Luke Combs, Cody Johnson, Ella Langley, Chris Stapleton, and Lainey Wilson are all battling it out in the Entertainer of the Year category.

For a full list of nominees, check out the CMA Awards website.

A Swift return

For the first time in 10 years, Taylor Swift will be attending the CMA Awards.

She is nominated for Single of the Year for her Toy Story 5 jam “I Knew It, I Knew You.” Swifties rejoice because the news doesn’t end there. She will also perform for the first time in 13 years.

Who is hosting the 60th CMA Awards?

Guiding the audience through all the awards, performances, and tributes is host Lainey Wilson. This is the third year in a row she has had the honor of MCing the event.

Wilson will be backed up by a slew of presenters. Martina McBride, Glen Powell, Carly Pearce, Michael Bublé, Joe Buck, Jessica Chastain, and Shaboozey are just some of the stars helping hand out the awards.

Additionally, Matt Rife, Luke Bryan, and Lara Spencer are also scheduled to appear.

Who is performing at the 60th CMA Awards?

Swift is far from the only performer to grace the stage. It is a night celebrating country music, after all.

Miranda Lambert, Ella Langley, Tim McGraw, Kacey Musgraves, Luke Combs, Vince Gill, Mumford & Sons, and Chris Stapleton are just some of the big names singing their hearts out.

As part of her hosting duties, Wilson will lead a Dolly Parton tribute in the opening of the show.

Parton passed away in August of this year. The beloved singer has had many celebrations of her incredible legacy including, “CMA Presents: I Will Always Love You: A Celebration of Dolly Parton.” Wilson believes Parton deserved every remembrance possible.

“No amount of honoring will be enough for that lady, and what she has done for this genre, what she has done for the world, what she did for me personally, the friend that she became,” Wilson told Robin Roberts on Good Morning America.

What award is Brooks & Dunn being presented with?

Since hitting the country music scene in 1991 with their hit single “Brand New Man,” Brooks & Dunn have been a fixture in country music.

The duo have won 20 CMA Awards, including Vocal Duo of the Year. At the 60th Annual CMA Awards, they will be presented with the Willie Nelson Lifetime Achievement Award.

Part of this honor is a special performance from the Brothers Osborne, Luke Bryan, Halestorm, HARDY, and Marcus King.

How can I watch or stream the awards live?

To catch all action, tune into ABC at 8 p.m. ET. This covers anyone with an over-the-air antenna and reception, meaning you can watch it live for free the old-fashioned way or via cable TV. And cord-cutters, rejoice. For the first time ever, the CMA Awards will also simulcast live on the Disney+ streaming service.

#10224. Thanksgiving dinner will cost more this year, Farm Bureau says

Record turkey prices and higher fuel costs could make Thanksgiving dinner more expensive this year, according to a survey released Wednesday.

The American Farm Bureau Federation said the cost of an average Thanksgiving feast for 10 will rise 6% from last year, to $58.63. The group tracks grocery prices using hundreds of volunteers in all 50 states and Puerto Rico.

The Farm Bureau, which has been tracking Thanksgiving costs for 40 years, said it’s the first time since 2022 that Americans will see the price of the meal increase. The price hit a record of $64.05 in 2022.

High diesel prices have made it more expensive for farmers to process and transport Thanksgiving staples like milk, dinner rolls, potatoes, and cranberries, the Farm Bureau said. Diesel prices have surged since the start of the Iran war and hit a record average of $6.53 per gallon in the U.S. in September, according to AAA.

On Wednesday, diesel averaged $5.96 per gallon, up 58% from a year ago, AAA said.

Turkey prices have also risen sharply over the past year. The Farm Bureau said the 16-pound turkey in its survey cost an average of $23.68 this year, up from $21.50 last year.

Bird flu has been decimating U.S. turkey flocks since an outbreak began in 2022. But cases have been waning, and turkey production increased substantially this year, said Mark Jordan, the executive director of Leap Market Analytics.

At the same time, turkey demand has been rising, as more Americans seek out lean protein and U.S. turkey exports rise. That strong demand has limited U.S. turkey inventories and raised prices. The U.S. Department of Agriculture expects the wholesale price of a whole frozen turkey hen will average a record $1.76 per pound this year, up 29% from last year.

“Over the last few years, there’s been a lot of doom and gloom for the turkey industry,” Jordan said. “This is one of those years that turkey producers are feeling a little bit better about their lot in life.”

Jordan said diesel costs likely didn’t impact turkey prices this year, since so much of the decision-making and timing related to the turkeys that will be consumed this Thanksgiving happened before diesel prices spiraled. But diesel costs could have a notable impact on turkey prices next year, he said.

A few of the items on the Thanksgiving menu are cheaper than last year, the Farm Bureau said. A 1-pound vegetable tray featuring carrots and celery is 5 cents cheaper, while a 16-ounce bag of frozen peas is 4 cents cheaper. Frozen pie crusts are also slightly cheaper, although a can of pumpkin pie filling is more expensive.

And in some cases, stores will price turkey and other Thanksgiving staples lower in order to draw shoppers. Aldi said its feast for 10, which mirrors the Farm Bureau’s menu, costs $39 this year. Walmart, which adds items like corn muffin mix and marshmallows but doesn’t include carrots and celery, said its feast for 10 is $35.

Persistently high grocery prices have been frustrating Americans since the pandemic and played a role in Republicans’ recent losses in the midterm elections. Prices for food eaten at home jumped 22% between October 2021 and October 2026, according to U.S. government data. That’s almost double the usual pace of food price inflation.

This year, the USDA predicts prices for food eaten at home to rise 2.3%. That would be lower than the recent annual average of 2.6%.

—By Dee-Ann Durbin, AP business writer

#10223. Granite 4.1 LLMs: How They’re Built

An in-depth technical walkthrough of data engineering, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning behind the Granite 4.1 LLMs.

TL;DR — Granite 4.1 is a family of dense, decoder‑only LLMs (3B, 8B, and 30B) trained on ~15T tokens using a multi‑stage pre‑training pipeline, including long‑context extension of up to 512K tokens. The models are further refined with supervised fine‑tuning on ~4.1M high‑quality curated samples and reinforcement learning via on‑policy GRPO with DAPO loss (Yu et al., 2025). Notably, the 8B instruct model matches or surpasses the previous Granite 4.0‑H‑Small (32B‑A9B MoE) despite using a simpler dense architecture with fewer parameters. All Granite 4.1 models are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Building high‑quality small language models goes beyond simply scaling compute—it requires rigorous data curation throughout training. For Granite 4.1, we prioritized data quality over quantity, progressively refining the data mixture across five pre‑training stages. We further curated supervised fine‑tuning data using an LLM‑as‑Judge framework and applied a multi‑stage reinforcement learning pipeline to systematically strengthen performance in math, coding, instruction following, and general chat.

Granite 4.1 models use a decoder-only dense transformer architecture. The core design choices include Grouped Query Attention (GQA), Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), SwiGLU activations, RMSNorm, and shared input/output embeddings.

All three model sizes share the same training pipeline and data strategy, differing only in architecture dimensions.

Granite 4.1 is trained from scratch on approximately 15 trillion tokens using a five‑phase training strategy. Phases 1–2 focus on foundational pre‑training, phases 3–4 perform mid‑training with progressively higher‑quality data annealing, and phase 5 introduces long‑context training, extending the context window to 512K tokens. Each phase employs a distinct data mixture and learning‑rate schedule, gradually shifting from broad web‑scale data to more curated, domain‑specific content.

Figure 2: The five-phase pre-training pipeline. Phases 1–2 are pre-training, Phases 3–4 are mid-training (high-quality data annealing), and Phase 5 is long context training (LCE).

The first phase establishes broad language understanding using a general mixture of training data with a power learning rate schedule and warmup.

Phase 2 sharply increases the proportion of code and mathematical data, pivoting toward stronger reasoning capabilities while still maintaining general language coverage.

Phase 3 transitions into mid-training with a more balanced, high-quality mixture and an exponential decay learning rate schedule. This is where we start blending in chain-of-thought and synthetic instruction data.

The fourth phase continues mid-training with a linear learning rate decay to zero, focusing the model on the highest-quality data available.

Figure 3: How the data mix evolves across the pre-training phases. Notice the progressive shift from web-heavy (Phase 1) to quality-heavy with instruction and reasoning data (Phases 3–4).

The fifth and final phase also part of of mid-training extends the context window from 4K to 512K through a staged long-context extension process:

The LCE phase uses an exponential learning rate schedule starting at 1e-4 and decaying to 0. To ensure the model natively handles long sequences without degrading short-context performance, we do a model merge after each LCE stage. RULER benchmark of base models:

Supervised fine‑tuning (SFT) is what turns the base model into a reliable instruction‑following assistant, making data quality critically important—since even a small number of incorrect or hallucinated samples can instill undesirable behaviors. To address this, we apply a rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework alongside rule‑based filtering to curate high-quality samples. Together, the pipeline automatically assess each sample against structural, semantic, and behavioral criteria, fixing issues when possible and filtering out samples that fail to meet our quality standards.

Figure 4: The SFT data quality pipeline. Raw conversation data passes through an LLM-as-Judge with a multi-dimensional rubric, producing accept/borderline/reject verdicts. Hard-reject defects (hallucination, false premise, incorrect computation) trigger automatic rejection regardless of score.

Our rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework evaluates only assistant responses, treating system prompts, user inputs, retrieved documents, and tool outputs strictly as contextual information. This ensures that the judge assesses what the model says, rather than what it was asked to do. In RAG settings, responses that are not grounded in the retrieved context are flagged as hallucinations, while tool‑use outputs are validated against the set of allowed tools and their parameter schemas.

We employ specialized judge prompts tailored to different SFT data types, including multi‑turn dialogue, RAG‑augmented responses, tool‑calling interactions, and multilingual conversations. Each response is scored across six weighted dimensions—instruction following, correctness, completeness, conciseness, naturalness, and calibration (with optional critical‑thinking checks). Samples are accepted, flagged as borderline, or rejected based on deterministic score thresholds, with hard‑reject rules overriding scores for severe defects such as hallucinations, false premises, or incorrect computations.

To complement semantic evaluation, we apply a deterministic rule‑based pipeline that enforces structural integrity through text normalization, truncation and length filtering, schema validation, and leakage detection. A final global deduplication step ensures dataset‑wide uniqueness. All filtering and correction actions are fully auditable.

After passing through the LLM-as-Judge, rule-based filtering, and global deduplication pipeline, we fine-tune base models on these approximately 4.1 million high-quality samples. The following details apply to all three model variants:

After SFT, we apply a multi-stage reinforcement learning pipeline to further improve the model's capabilities across specific domains. Rather than a single RL pass, we run multiple targeted RL stages, each optimizing for different capabilities.

We use On-policy GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) (Shao et al., 2024) with DAPO (Decoupled Clip and Dynamic sAmpling Policy Optimization) loss (Yu et al., 2025) which provides more stable training signals compared to standard GRPO. However, due to computationally intensive nature of dynamic sampling, we switch it off during our training runs.

Figure 10 depicts our Reinforcement Learning pipeline for training Granite 4.1 models. Through extensive experimentation with a variety of reinforcement learning recipes, we found that this sequence of steps minimizes catastrophic forgetting while simultaneously maximizing performance across multiple domains.

Figure 10: The Granite 4.1 reinforcement learning pipeline consisting of four sequential stages: Multi-domain RL, RLHF, Identity and Knowledge-calibration RL, and Math RL.

In this stage, the model is trained jointly on a unified mixture of data drawn from multiple domains. Every gradient update therefore reflects the full diversity of tasks, which prevents catastrophic forgetting, boosts overall benchmark performance, and minimizes regressions on any individual task.

The different domains covered in this stage include:

During this stage, we trained the models on 45,504 unique prompts (averaged across all Granite 4.1 models) and found that a learning rate of 5e‑7 with a KL‑loss coefficient ($\beta$) of 0.05 performed best for multi‑domain reinforcement learning.

To further improve the model's helpfulness and chat ability, we train our model on generic-chat prompts using a multilingual scalar reward model. With this stage, we observed an average improvement of ~18.9 points (averaged across the three Granite 4.1 models) in Alpaca-Eval compared to the SFT checkpoints.

To mitigate policy drift from its previously learned knowledge, we use a conservative learning rate of 3e-7 and higher KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09 in this stage. We use an average of 17,920 unique prompts in this RLHF stage.

In this stage, we train the model for a few steps (~40 training steps) on identity and knowledge calibration prompts. We observed that this small training stage significantly improves the model's self-identification capabilities.

Similar to the RLHF stage, we used a learning rate of 3e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09, and we use 1728 unique prompts in this stage.

During our RL training, we found that the RLHF stage causes a drop in math benchmark scores (e.g., in GSM8K, DeepMind-Math). The Math RL stage enables the model to recover from this drop and surpasses the original SFT performance on math benchmarks: ~3.8 points on average for GSM8K, and ~23.48 points on average for DeepMind-Math. We use an average of 13,504 unique prompts in this stage and similar to the multi-domain RL stage, we used a learning rate of 5e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.05.

Supported languages: English, German, Spanish, French, Japanese, Portuguese, Arabic, Czech, Italian, Korean, Dutch, and Chinese.

Granite 4.1 delivers competitive instruction‑following and tool‑calling capabilities without relying on long chains of thought. By avoiding extended reasoning traces, it provides predictable latency, stable token usage, and lower operational cost. This makes Granite 4.1 a production‑ready, open‑source choice for enterprise workloads where efficiency, reliability, and cost control are critical.

A striking result: the Granite 4.1-8B dense model consistently matches or outperforms the previous-generation Granite 4.0-H-Small, a 32B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 9B active parameters.

Figure 13: Granite 4.1-8B (dark blue) vs. Granite 4.0-H-Small 32B-A9B (light blue) across benchmarks. The 8B dense model matches or exceeds the larger MoE model on IFEval, AlpacaEval, MMLU-Pro, BBH, GSM8K, DeepMind-Math, Evalplus, ArenaHard, BFCL V3 and MBPP(+).

Figure 14: Comparison across the Granite 4.1 family — 30B, 8B, and 3B models. Scores scale predictably with model size, with the 30B model leading across all benchmarks.

We also released fp8 quantized variants of the Granite 4.1 models, optimized for inference with vLLM. The precision is reduced from 16‑bit to 8‑bit, resulting in approximately a 50% reduction in both disk footprint and GPU memory usage. Quantization is applied only to the weights and activations of linear operators within the transformer blocks using LLM Compressor, while all other layers are preserved at their original precision.

We trained the Granite 4.1 Language Models on an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 cluster hosted on CoreWeave:

This infrastructure provides the scalable, high-bandwidth interconnect needed for efficient distributed training at the token volumes required (15T+ tokens across pre-training alone).

Granite 4.1 models are available under the Apache 2.0 license. Here's how to get started with the 30B instruct model wiht tool calling example:

Granite 4.1 marks a significant step forward for high‑quality, open‑source language models. By prioritizing data quality and rigor at every stage—from pre‑training curation to supervised fine‑tuning and multi‑stage reinforcement learning—we deliver a substantially improved post‑training pipeline. The result is stronger instruction following, tool use, and conversational performance, showing that carefully trained dense 8B models can rival much larger MoE architectures. We’re excited to see how the community adopts and builds on these models.

A small but welcome potential reprieve for PC builders and consumers.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Solid-state drives, phones, laptops, and tablets have all gotten substantially pricier in the last couple of years. Beyond the stratospheric prices of DDR5 memory, prospective PC builders and consumer electronics buyers have had to deal with upcharges on SSDs of all sizes thanks to the AI boom. That may be changing soon, as spot pricing for consumer NAND chips is reportedly dropping, according to a new report from Seoul Economic Daily (SED).

The report observes a 20% drop in spot pricing for NAND chips over just the last month. Its conclusions are bolstered by information from a Bank of America note from Nov. 13, wherein industry sources tell that institution that NAND is due for a market correction.

SED says that according to that note, 512 Gb NAND wafers saw a 32% drop to $14.30 apiece on the spot market, while 1 Tb wafers fell 19% to $24.90. SED quotes another industry source that says: "NAND cannot sustain the steep price gains seen so far."

Those decreases may be hard to square in a time when enterprise SSDs are getting pricier by the day, but SED notes that the rise in phone and PC prices has led customers to delay upgrades, resulting in a 20% year-on-year decline in shipments for phones alone and making for the lowest third-quarter volumes in 14 years. Meanwhile, PC shipments have also fallen 22.5% year-on-year, according to a Gartner report.

In the face of those consumer decisions, device makers are letting their existing stock drain out and are presumably stocked with NAND chips for the short term, thus resulting in lower prices for new fab shipments on the short-term spot market.

Another factor in the consumer NAND market is that not all flash is equal. Both RAM and NAND makers have been redirecting their chip output to serve the ongoing AI boom, converting their consumer-grade production lines to make higher-spec silicon. Memory factories have been converting DDR5 capacity to HBM at a steady pace, as parts of the process are shared across both types.

But according to the Bank of America note that SED cites, things are different in the NAND world. High-density flash now sits at around 300 layers, and its production requires substantially different tooling compared to the lower-grade silicon deemed suitable for us mere mortals. So the continuing growth in NAND demand from AI data centers may not translate directly into reduced consumer supply.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Beyond those factors, added supply from Chinese NAND maker YMTC is creating additional downward price pressure in the NAND market. SED notes that YMTC has taken a 14% chunk from major players in the NAND market in the second quarter of this year alone.

On net, these forces could result in a bit of relief for consumer tech. SED says Bank of America expects consumer NAND prices for PCs and smartphones to fall 5% to 10% on the longer-term contract market in the first quarter of 2027, while enterprise NAND contract prices are expected to hold more or less steady.

Whether those declines translate to lower prices for finished devices and components like SSDs will remain to be seen, and products with those chips inside will require some time to reach the market. But in the ongoing AI supply crunch, any potential relief is worth celebrating.

#10220. The Ikea shopping experience is about to look very different

Ikea stores are known for being so massive that they make furniture shopping feel like a bit of a journey. Albeit, one with meatballs. But the brand is expanding on a whole new, and noticeably sleeker, shopping experience for its customers.

Ingka Group, the world’s largest Ikea franchisee, says its “big blue box” stores aren’t going anywhere. However, smaller stores—which debuted in Los Angeles in 2025—will start popping up in more cities in 2027. The expansion will also include more plan-and-order points, where customers seeking design and planning advice can go.

“The big blue box will remain the backbone,” Ingka CEO Juvencio Maeztu, who came on board last year, told Reuters. The CEO added: “We are adding smaller formats for convenience, either because you don’t have an ​Ikea in your city, or you have one but you want a bit more convenience on a ​weekly and monthly basis.” 

The announcement comes amid struggling sales for the brand. On November 6, Ikea reported its third straight year of declining sales—down about 2% across 64 countries compared with last year—as consumers are increasingly cutting larger purchases and nonessential items from their budgets.

“We are determined to make Ikea even more affordable and accessible for the many people. Our business model is built on a simple idea: High volumes and low costs enable us to offer low prices,” Jakub Jankowski, CEO of Inter Ikea, which owns ​the Ikea brand, said in the report.

Jankowski added: “Sales have remained stable in recent years, despite challenging market conditions. But to reach more people with affordable home furnishings, we need to return to growth. In FY26, we took important steps to strengthen the business, create the conditions for growth, and enable us to lower prices even further.”

In a previous announcement, Ikea was already laying out plans for how to accomplish its goals. The brand explained that it has been amplifying efforts to meet the needs of the modern furniture shopper. It said it would add nine small-format stores, which carry Ikea’s full range of products. It also said it would add 10 plan-and-order points with pickup, which give customers a more personalized experience, and 10 new meeting points inside Best Buy locations.

In September, the brand also announced it would invest $1.39 billion (1.2 billion euros) in price cuts for European customers amid declining sales. 

The iconic brand has already opened a number of new U.S. stores this year, including locations in Chantilly, Virginia; Huntsville, Alabama; Phoenix; Newnan, Georgia; Escondido/San Diego, California; and Tulsa, Oklahoma. It opened its final big-blue-box store for the year in Sarasota, Florida, on November 18.

Ikea also recently opened three new small-format stores in Texas (Dallas/University Park, Rockwall, and Webster). And it aims to open at least seven new small-format stores next year. The planned locations include Fort Collins, Colorado; Gurnee, Illinois; Naperville, Illinois; Buffalo, New York; Westlake, Ohio; New York City; and Madison, Wisconsin.

#10219. Adding Benchmaxxer Repellant to the Open ASR Leaderboard

"When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." (Goodhart’s Law)

TLDR: Appen Inc. and DataoceanAI have provided high-quality English ASR datasets covering scripted and conversational speech over multiple accents. To prevent potential risks of benchmaxxing or test-set contamination, we will keep these datasets private for a high-quality measure of performance on multiple tasks.

We’re not updating the average WER at this time: by default, the leaderboard’s Average WER remains computed on public datasets only. You can optionally include the private datasets using the toggle to see their impact 👀

Since its launch in September 2023, the Open ASR Leaderboard has been visited over 710K times. We’re blown away by the community’s interest and motivation to keep pushing speech recognition 🗣️

Two words sum up the objectives (but also challenges) in maintaining a benchmark like the Open ASR Leaderboard:

Standardization: models can have different conventions for their usage and outputs, e.g. with/without punctuation and casing. Datasets have the same challenges and can be structured differently. To this end, all test sets have been gathered into a single dataset on the Hub for easy access and previewing. Moreover, to standardize model outputs and dataset transcripts, we use a normalizer that (among other things) removes punctuation and casing, and maps to American spelling. It is based on the normalizer of Whisper.

Openness: the UI code and evaluation scripts are open-sourced. This has helped not only to incorporate new models, but also to improve the quality of the evaluation procedure through community feedback and contributions.

Standardization and openness are essential for meaningful benchmarking, but they also make benchmarks more susceptible to benchmark-specific optimization ("benchmaxxing"), where models improve leaderboard performance without corresponding gains in real-world robustness. As models and use cases evolve, the Open ASR Leaderboard will continue incorporating high-quality datasets and new evaluation settings to better reflect real-world performance and improve robustness against benchmark-specific optimization.

As discussed in our report, there is no single "catch-all" ASR model: some perform better on American English, others on diverse accents and multilingual settings, while others are optimized for speed or conversational audio. Different applications also prioritize different capabilities, so a model that performs less well on one dimension is not necessarily a worse model overall. The goal of the Open ASR Leaderboard is to capture these nuances and provide a more holistic view of ASR performance.

To this end, we have worked with Appen Inc. and DataoceanAI to curate high-quality datasets for ASR benchmarking. Below is some information on the various splits.

Below are sample audio showing the variety of content (scripted, conversational, acronyms, disfluencies, proper nouns).

While private datasets may sound contrary to the spirit of openness, we believe that incorporating such datasets will increase the trustworthiness of the Open ASR Leaderboard, as they are less likely to be exploited for benchmaxxing, whether by model developers who explicitly use the public test sets or who try to find training data that closely resembles a particular dataset to boost their score in the macroaverage.

With these datasets, we can also provide targeted metrics to highlight gaps and biases between controlled and often saturated settings (scripted, American accent) and more nuanced conditions (conversational and non-American accents). Below is a screenshot of the new "Private data" tab.

We intentionally do not provide a score on each split, to avoid model developers from boosting their score with a specific data provider or accent.

Get your model on the Open ASR Leaderboard, and we'll run the evaluation! As before, the process for adding a model to the leaderboard takes place on the Open ASR Leaderboard GitHub:

While you wait for your model to be added to the Open ASR Leaderboard, you can self-report your metrics on the public sets by adding a YAML file like this to your model card. Your model will then appear on an (unverified) leaderboard that appears on the dataset page (see screenshot below). More on this approach to decentralized evaluation can be read here.

They could. We’ve asked Appen and DataoceanAI to not provide this data to their clients. But even if they do not provide this exact data, data from a similar distribution could still help the model on the corresponding evaluation set (similar to benchmaxxing by optimizing for a challenging task from the public sets). To this end, having multiple data providers balances out the advantage a model may get from having used data from one of the providers. And we are open to more data providers and eval sets for the "Private data" tab!

Moreover, to ensure that the private sets do not affect the model ranking, we’ve defaulted the Average WER to not include the Private sets in its macroaverage.

In the screenshot below, you can see that "Private data" is toggled off. This means that the macroaverage across datasets does not include it.

Simply toggle on "Private data" splits to include them in the macroaverage.

The "Rank Δ" column shows how the ordering changes relative to the default macroaverage configuration. Including or excluding public datasets also changes the macroaverage, allowing users to tailor the evaluation to the use cases and data distributions most relevant to their application.

We’re excited to hear the community’s feedback on how the new track and dataset toggling features help users identify the model(s) that best fit their application(s). We’re also looking into evaluations that better reflect real-world noisy conditions, and you can expect some news on that 😉

While preparing the private evaluation sets, we took extra care to ensure consistent audio and transcript quality across datasets, including developing tooling to identify challenging cases such as low signal-to-noise conditions or transcript mismatches, since these factors can meaningfully affect WER. More on that in a future post!

Explore and compare speech‑to‑text model benchmarks

Just a quick observation on how we evaluate our models: The two data vendors mentioned earlier are offering datasets directly to ASR service providers for training. With that in mind, it feels like we should be extra prudent about mixing private data into our evaluations.

At the same time, we're missing out on a lot of high-quality, open-source speech datasets simply because their creators don't have sales teams advocating for them. It would be a huge step forward to open a channel where the research community can recommend these datasets to the leaderboard directly.

P.S. I found myself relating a lot to King George in the movie Hoppers recently. That beaver king just believes the best about everyone. I want to bring that same optimism here—hoping that everyone continues to follow the leaderboard rules, avoids training on open-source test sets, and actively cleans their training data of any contamination.

#10218. Automating Contract Signing in Node.js: Webhooks, Verification, and Storing Signed PDFs

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sending a document for signature is the easy part of an e-signature integration. One POST request and the signer gets an email. The work that actually breaks in production happens afterwards: knowing when the document was signed, trusting the notification that told you so, handling the same notification twice, and getting the final PDF into storage before the download link expires.

This tutorial builds that whole loop in Node.js with Express. An event in your app (a deal is approved, a client is onboarded, a task moves to "ready to sign") sends a contract from a template. When the signer finishes, a webhook arrives, your server verifies it, and the signed PDF plus its audit trail get saved without anyone touching them.

The code uses Firma.dev, the e-signature API I work on, because I needed a real API to make the examples runnable. The patterns are not specific to it, though. Signature verification, idempotent handlers, short-lived download URLs, and reconciliation jobs show up in almost every webhook-driven integration, and the same structure applies whether you're receiving events from a payment processor, a CI system, or another signing provider.

There's a fifth part that tutorials usually skip: a reconciliation job that catches anything the webhooks missed. We'll build that too, because webhooks are a notification mechanism, not a delivery guarantee.

Before sending anything, wrap the HTTP calls in one place. This is where authentication lives, and it's also where you handle 429 Too Many Requests once instead of in every caller. Most APIs, this one included, return a Retry-After header on a 429, so the client should honour it rather than guessing a backoff.

The 503 branch matters later. When a document has just been completed, the final PDF and its completion certificate take a moment to generate, and the download endpoint says so with a 503 and a Retry-After instead of handing you a half-built file.

The trigger depends on your product. It might be a route handler, a queue consumer, or a CRM automation calling into your service. What matters is that the function doing the sending is small and takes plain data:

Two design choices are worth calling out.

Use a single create-and-send call when you can. Many signing APIs split this into "create a draft" and "send the draft." That's useful when a human needs to review the document first, but for automation it creates a window where your process can crash between the two calls and leave an orphaned draft. A combined endpoint makes the operation atomic from your side.

Store the provider's ID on your own record immediately. Webhook payloads reference the signing request, not your deal or customer. Without that mapping you'll end up searching by email address, which falls apart as soon as one client signs two documents.

Here's the first place integrations quietly go wrong. Webhook signatures are computed over the exact bytes the sender transmitted. If Express parses the body as JSON first, you lose those bytes, and re-serialising the object won't reproduce them (key order, whitespace, and number formatting can all change). Signature checks then fail intermittently, which is the worst kind of failure.

The fix is to use express.raw() on the webhook route only, so the handler receives a Buffer:

Most webhook providers sign payloads with HMAC-SHA256 using a shared secret. The details vary, so read your provider's docs for the exact header format, but the scheme here is common: the header looks like t=1731456000,v1=5f2b..., and the signed string is the timestamp, a dot, and the raw body. Stripe uses a very similar format, and the Standard Webhooks spec describes the same idea as a vendor-neutral convention.

Each line here defends against something specific.

The OWASP guidance on cryptographic storage covers the other half of this: the secret belongs in an environment variable or secrets manager, never in the repository.

Every serious webhook system delivers at least once, not exactly once. If your endpoint is slow, returns a 5xx, or the network drops the response, the sender retries. Firma.dev, for example, makes up to three attempts per event (immediately, then after at least five minutes, then after at least an hour) and treats anything other than a 2xx as a failure, including redirects. Other providers retry more aggressively. Either way, your handler will eventually see the same event twice.

The defence is to record each event's unique ID and skip ones you've seen. In the server above that's alreadyProcessed and markProcessed. For a demo, a Set works:

In production, use your database and let a unique constraint do the work, so two concurrent deliveries can't both pass the check:

Also notice the order in the route: respond with 200, then do the work. Many providers time out deliveries after a few seconds (five, in this case). Downloading a PDF and uploading it to object storage can easily take longer than that, and a timeout counts as a failure, which triggers a retry, which triggers duplicate work. Acknowledging fast and processing asynchronously avoids that loop.

setImmediate is fine for a tutorial, but it has a real weakness: if the process dies after sending the 200 and before finishing the work, the event is acknowledged and lost. In production, push the event onto a durable queue (BullMQ, SQS, a jobs table) before responding. Step 7 covers the safety net for whatever still slips through.

Now the actual business logic. You'll usually see several event types (sent, viewed, a signer signed, declined, expired, completed). Only one of them means "the document is final":

Three things in here are easy to get wrong.

Don't treat "a signer signed" as "the document is done." With multiple signers, each one triggers its own event, and a per-signer "all complete" flag can be true on more than one of them. Key your storage logic off the single completion event.

Don't persist the download URL. Pre-signed URLs expire (this one carries an expires_at). Saving the link to your database and serving it to users later produces broken links a few minutes or hours later. Download the bytes and store them in storage you control. Swapping the fs.writeFile calls for an S3 PutObject or a Google Drive upload is a drop-in change.

Store the audit trail, not just the PDF. If a signature is ever disputed, the PDF shows what was signed, and the audit trail shows who signed it, when, and from where (timestamps, IP addresses, the sequence of views and signatures). That evidence is what makes an electronic signature defensible, which brings us to the legal side.

Retries are finite. Endpoints go down during deploys. Some providers auto-disable a webhook after enough consecutive failures, and events aren't guaranteed to arrive in order. Any one of these can leave a completed document sitting unsaved.

A small scheduled job closes that gap. Keep a list of signing requests your app considers "pending," and periodically ask the API for their real status:

Since storeSignedDocument overwrites by ID, running it twice for the same document is harmless. That's the property you want from every step in a webhook pipeline: doing it again shouldn't change the result.

None of this is legal advice, but a few facts shape how you build.

In the US, the ESIGN Act and the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (adopted by 49 states) give electronic signatures the same legal standing as handwritten ones for most commercial documents. ESIGN also has requirements around consumer consent and record retention, which is part of why you store the final PDF yourself rather than relying on a third-party link.

In the EU, eIDAS defines three levels: simple (SES), advanced (AdES), and qualified (QES). SES and AdES cover most business contracts. QES requires a qualified trust service provider and certificate-based identity, and some documents (certain property transfers and court filings, depending on the country) require it or exclude e-signatures entirely. Check which level your document types need before you pick a provider, since not every API offers every level.

Across jurisdictions, the evidence that holds up is the same: who signed, how they were identified, when it happened, and proof the document hasn't changed since. That's the audit trail and the completion certificate, which is why Step 6 stores both.

If you're evaluating providers for a workflow like this, the questions that matter at the integration level are mostly not on the pricing page:

The send call is one line. The reliability comes from everything around it: keeping the raw body for verification, checking timestamps and comparing in constant time, acknowledging fast and deduplicating by event ID, downloading files before their links expire, and running a reconciliation job for the events that never arrive. Get those right and contract signing becomes something your app does in the background, with no one chasing signatures or copying PDFs between folders.

For the Firma.dev-specific details used here (event names, header format, rate limits), see the webhooks guide.

#10217. Flight canceled? Capital One will now let some travelers switch airlines for free

Flight delays and cancellations can be a headache for anyone, but for business travelers, a disrupted flight can also mean missed meetings and potentially missed deals.

Capital One is introducing a new perk designed to make those disruptions a little easier to manage. Starting Wednesday, select Capital One Business customers can receive complimentary flight disruption rebooking on flights purchased through Capital One Business Travel.

When your original flight is canceled or significantly delayed, the limited-time benefit allows eligible travelers to book a replacement flight on any airline at no additional cost, up to $5,000 per traveler. For instance, if your First Class flight on United gets canceled due to a maintenance issue, you can rebook a First Class ticket on Delta for no additional cost.

“Business owners and professionals often operate on tight schedules, and travel disruptions can have a significant impact on productivity,” said Natalie Conners, senior business director of Capital One Business Travel. “While delays and cancellations are often unavoidable, the stress and uncertainty they create don’t have to be.”

How Capital One’s free flight rebooking works

The complimentary benefit is automatically added at checkout when eligible customers book flights through Capital One Business Travel.

Capital One will start monitoring those flights 24 hours before departure. If a flight is canceled or delayed by at least three hours on the day of travel, travelers receive a notification giving them access to a self-service rebooking tool.

Flights can be rebooked for the same or following day, and must be in the same or a lower fare class and arrive at the original destination or a nearby airport. The benefit covers disruptions caused by weather, airport operations, and air traffic control issues, among other circumstances.

Travelers can rebook digitally without speaking to an agent, although Capital One also offers 24/7 live travel support.

Who qualifies for complimentary rebooking?

The promotion is available to select Capital One Business customers booking through Capital One Business Travel through the end of January 2027, while supplies last.

Cardholders can check their eligibility by logging into the Capital One Business Travel platform through their business account. Customers who don’t qualify for the complimentary offer can still purchase flight disruption assistance through Capital One Business Travel or Capital One Travel.

The new perk builds on Capital One’s existing business travel platform, which allows cardholders and their employees to book flights, hotels, and rental cars, earn loyalty rewards, and manage company travel expenses.

For eligible business travelers heading into the busy holiday travel season, the biggest advantage may be having more options when a flight goes wrong.

#10215. America’s rental market just hit a surprising turning point. Here’s what it means for your rent

Depending on where you live, this might seem unbelievable, but rents have actually come down in many places in the past year.

Across the 50 largest U.S. metro areas, the median asking rent increased only $1 from last year, to $1,692 in October for studio, one- and two-bedroom properties, according to a new report from Realtor.com. This marks only the first annual increase in median rents in more than three years, as 26 major metro areas have actually seen rents fall in the past year, according to data from the Austin-based real estate site.

Of course, location matters. The story of today’s rent prices depends largely on how robust the construction boom was earlier this decade—and how many projects are in the pipeline. That’s why many renters may not feel like they’re seeing much relief.

“Renters still face a very different affordability picture than they did before the pandemic,” Jiayi Xu, senior economist at Realtor.com, said in a statement. “Elevated borrowing costs may keep more households renting, just as new deliveries slow. That makes the local construction pipeline increasingly important to the outlook for rent relief.”

WHERE RENTS ARE FALLING

Amid a broader affordability crisis, rents have been somewhat contained in recent years. Median asking rents nationwide fell for three straight years thanks largely to a boom in multi-family construction projects between 2021 and 2022 that added supply to the rental market.

Nationwide, it’s been a good run for people who don’t mind small living, as the median rent for a studio fell 1.2% in the past year to $1,411 as of October, according to Realtor.com. That marked the 39th consecutive month of annual declines in studio rents.

Renters in the South have experienced the most rent relief, as the metro areas that saw the biggest declines in median rent in the past year were:

  • San Antonio, Texas: Down 3.7% to $1,117
  • Tampa, Florida: Down 2.3% to $1,604
  • Nashville, Tennessee: Down 2.1% to $1,504
  • Houston, Texas: Down 1.9% to $1,377
  • Detroit, Michigan: Down 1.8% to $1,146
  • Sacramento, California: Down 1.8% to $1,794

Though rents edged up in Oklahoma City, this metro area holds the distinction for being the only in the latest report where the median rent is below $1,000, at $956.

WHERE RENTS ARE RISING

As has been true with the broader housing market, the current rental situation and outlook is a tale of four regions. And yet, renters nationwide may need to brace for potential rent increases ahead.

The Northeast has recently entered a rebuilding phase of the construction cycle, but given the lag when those projects will be delivered, rents could continue to rise. Meanwhile, the Midwest has the largest pipeline of projects relative to pre-pandemic levels but still saw rent increases in the past year. Even in the South and West, which have rent prices continuing to come down in recent years, those declines are narrowing in some metro areas in the South and weaker construction activity in the West could limit the relief to renters in that region.

Renters who want more space to stretch their legs or because of their familial needs are seeing the biggest increases in monthly rent. For the first time in more than three years, the median rent for a two-bedroom increased on an annual basis, up 0.3% to $1,889 nationwide. These renters have seen prices surge by nearly 19% in the past seven years, compared with a median increase of 15% in that time across all unit sizes.

Renters in the Midwest and California’s greater Bay area are getting squeezed most, as the metro areas that saw the biggest increases in median rent in the past year were:

  • San Francisco, California: Up 6.3% to $3,094
  • San Jose, California: Up 6.2% to $3,540
  • Milwaukee, WIsconsin: Up 4.1% to $1,767

#10213. HBO Max is moving ahead with an Elon Musk documentary despite his $1 billion investment. Here’s why

Skydance CEO David Ellison says the company will honor the distribution deal to stream Alex Gibney’s Musk documentary, even after Elon Musk’s $1 billion investment in the company.

The nearly four-hour documentary on the Tesla and SpaceX executive is expected to hit the streamer in early 2027, but Musk’s recent investment had put into question whether HBO would air it.

HBO is now part of Skydance following the controversial merger between Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount earlier this year. While Bleecker Street and Universal hold the theatrical rights in the U.S. and internationally, respectively, HBO holds the streaming rights for the documentary. 

When asked about the potential conflict at the 2026 DealBook summit in New York on Wednesday, Ellison told New York Times columnist and DealBook founder Andrew Ross Sorkin that he intends to follow through with the commitment to A24.

“We believe in independence. We don’t believe in censorship of any kind,” Ellison told Sorkin. He added: “We have that deal with A24, and of course we’ll honor it.” 

According to Deadline, Ellison appears to have misattributed the deal to HBO’s pay-1 deal with A24, a multiyear licensing deal that gives HBO exclusive streaming rights to A24-made films. A pay-1 deal gives a premium cable network or streaming service the first window to exclusively air a film following its theatrical release. Pay-1 windows often last about 18 months, at which point other networks can acquire streaming rights.

Deadline reports that the deal Ellison refers to is most likely a commitment with HBO Documentary Films instead.

The statement from Ellison follows Musk’s own criticism of the documentary, which he referred to as a “hit piece.”

The documentary in question features interviews with figures from Musk’s life, including his first wife, Justine Musk; Tesla cofounder Martin Eberhard; and the mother of Musk’s 13th child, Ashley St. Clair. Additionally, figures from the entrepreneur and tech world are also featured in the film, including LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman and British Canadian computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton, also known as the “godfather of AI.”

Ellison also took the stage to praise Musk, calling him “the greatest entrepreneur of our time.”

He added: “To have his vote of confidence and to have him as a shareholder is an honor and a privilege. And if there was any opportunity to be able to collaborate with him in the future, from our perspective, it would be a privilege.”
