The most highly anticipated video game of the decade is here. GTA VI arrives almost 13 years after GTA V, with reports suggesting that it has already generated around $1.54 billion in revenue from 16 million preorders. Ahead of its release, Rockstar Games has finally shared some technical details, including rendering resolutions and upscaling technologies being used across all consoles.

In a statement shared with Wccftech, the technical team at Rockstar has confirmed that GTA VI uses different upscaling solutions across all consoles in order to achieve a balance between visual quality and performance with a target of 30FPS. The PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X use Rockstar's own temporal anti-aliasing (TAA) solution, while the PlayStation 5 Pro relies on Sony's second-generation PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR2). The Xbox Series S, meanwhile, relies on AMD's FSR 4 upscaling technology.

As for rendered resolutions, the PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X, and PlayStation 5 Pro all start with a native base resolution of 1440p, which is then upscaled to 4K. The Xbox Series S is the least powerful console; thus, the game runs at a lower base resolution of 720p, which is upscaled to 1080p using FSR 4. The final image on all consoles is then composited with a 4K user interface before being presented.

Rockstar has also developed a physically-based material library for GTA VI and a cinematic imaging pipeline to deliver realistic lighting, reflections, and material details within the game. The team says it has worked to maintain a consistent lighting solution across all consoles, including the Xbox Series S, while adjusting ray-traced global illumination (RTGI) features depending on each platform's hardware capabilities.

The PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S launched all the way back in 2020, and while the consoles have capable hardware, their architectures are finally beginning to show their age. The fact that Rockstar is targeting just 30FPS across all consoles, while relying on different upscaling technologies and rendering resolutions, highlights how much performance is potentially being left on the table in order to maintain visual fidelity. That being said, a PC release of GTA VI continues to be a big question mark. Rockstar is yet to announce a release date or even provide a launch window, meaning that PC gamers can only rely on Xbox Cloud Gaming to stream the game on their systems.

The 8BitDo 64 was a loose remake of the Nintendo 64’s unusual triple-grip controller that did away with that gamepad’s centered analog stick. But with its new GC Bluetooth Gamepad, 8BitDo has done a much better job at staying faithful to the design of the Nintendo GameCube’s excellent controllers, including their unique button layout, thumbstick design, and shoulder buttons.

The 8BitDo GC Bluetooth Gamepad is available for preorder starting today for $49.99 in orange or purple and is expected to start shipping on December 10th. That’s much cheaper than Nintendo’s $69.99 wireless remake of the GameCube controller, although 8BitDo’s version isn’t an exact copy of the original’s shape and ergonomics. If that’s important to you, and you have your GameCube’s original accessories on hand, you can still buy 8BitDo’s $25.98 upgrade kit, which is a cheaper way to make it compatible with modern consoles and devices.

8BitDo’s GameCube redux carries forward the original’s octagonal gates around the base of each thumbstick, making it well-suited to playing fighting games like Super Smash Bros. Ultimate. And while Nintendo continues to skip modern thumbstick technologies, the 8BitDo GC features both drift-resistant TMR thumbsticks and Hall effect linear triggers.

The controller connects to all versions of the Nintendo Switch over Bluetooth, as well as PCs or handheld consoles running Windows. It also comes with a 2.4GHz wireless USB receiver for players who prefer a connection with lower latency, or you can connect it with a USB-C cable for the best possible performance.

Besides removing the Samples tab, YouTube Music for Android and iOS is rolling out instant access to Ask Music with a new Gemini icon in the top-right corner.

The Gemini spark appears on almost every screen in the app, including the Home feed, Library tab, Now Playing, albums, and playlists. It matches Gemini in Gmail and other Workspace apps online, as well as Google Messages in a future update.

#10161. Beyond LLMs: Why Scalable Enterprise AI Adoption Depends on Agent Logic

Guides have aided humanity throughout history. Prehistoric civilizations understood that the sun and the moon could be used to navigate vast distances on land and the high seas. Over time, various journeys facilitated the production of maps for better planning and faster travel time to repeat destinations. Centuries later, the introduction of the compass enabled seagoers to achieve greater accuracy in seeking unexplored destinations. And today, GPS navigation apps guide our every journey. In today’s world of agentic AI, AI agents, admittedly, have the potential to enable scalable AI adoption, transforming industries as we know them. However, an intelligent guide, agentic logic, is needed to realize this potential by fueling high agent quality, cost-effectiveness, and consequent end-user trust.

Numerous studies have cited the overwhelming failure of AI pilots, while others have also highlighted the need for AI to operate at the core of enterprise workflows to enable scalable adoption. [1] [2] To better understand this phenomenon and the associated assertion, some analysis of enterprise workflows is required. These workflows are:

A. Dynamic and long-runningB. Possess a plethora of APIs, databases and servicesC. Oftentimes are constrained by business policies and/or regulations

For an agent to function effectively, given these above characteristics, naturally demands an expanded model context, which state-of-the-art frontier LLMs certainly possess, but at what tradeoff? Increased hallucinations, token consumption? Further, can LLMs be equipped with an intelligent guide, GPS, to enable agentic AI execution at the core of the workflow, driving more desirable outcomes? We tested these hypotheses by designing and building agents, equipped with pertinent agent logic, for IBM offerings fully considering the above characteristics. These offerings pertain to some of the most challenging tasks confronting subject matter experts who own various stages of the enterprise software delivery lifecycle for mission critical workloads including:

Before examining each of these domains in detail, let us define what characterizes agent logic. Agent logic is software primitives, such as knowledge graphs, algorithms, program analysis libraries, which operate at the agentic layer (within an agent harness) and can intentionally steer the LLM in the direction of the enterprise workflow, reducing the context space. In so doing, have strong tendency to drive more performant outcomes in a more cost-effective manner. Let us now examine how agent logic is able to achieve such outcomes in each of the above four domains.

IBM watsonx Code assistant for Z (WCA4Z), used to accelerate mainframe application development and modernization with AI and automation, is equipped with an App Insights agent for application understanding - one of the primary focus areas of enterprise clients running mission critical workloads on IBM mainframe. This agent leverages deep static analysis across the application and stores a pre-indexed representation in a database schema that spans hundreds of interrelated tables with complex semantics, allowing the agent to retrieve precise, structured already available information; thereby improving answer accuracy, reducing token usage, and minimizing back-and-forth interactions with the language model (Mistral Medium 250B in this instance). This approach when applied to multiple mission-critical legacy systems (up to 1M lines of code and 1K programs) maintains marginally superior app understanding performance with ~30× lower token consumption than a baseline frontier LLM-only approach.

Aster is an IBM proprietary program analysis and data pre- and post-processing-based library utilized for agent-based generation of unit, integration, API and change-based tests; which from analysis of multiple developer communities achieves higher developer ratings compared with various open-sourced tools or developer-written tests. Based on the latter and superior line, branch and method coverage benchmarks compared with similar open-sourced tools (integration tests) and zero-shot LLMs and coding agents (unit tests), all tested on open-sourced applications, we have been running Aster in pre-production mode on 75+ java IBM CIO applications (up to 560+ classes and 67K+ lines of code) with Devstral 24B model. Steady-state results to date yield +20% - 45% improvement in line, branch and method coverage coupled with superior performance on a subset of these apps compared with state-of-the-art coding agent with orders of magnitude lower token consumption (up to 15×). The rationale for these results is that the program analysis output (used to prompt and “focus” the LLM) coupled with sub-agents for augmenting coverage and remediating runtime and compilation errors enable a more performant outcome with significant cost reduction.

While LLM context for app-related use cases as described in 1 and 2 are “restricted” to the app source code, for runtime management of apps on deployed infra, the underlying IT full stack comes into play. Here we define a knowledge graph (KG) encompassing entities (microservices, database/middleware services, MELT etc.) coupled with embedded (“tribal”) knowledge from domain experts. With such a graph and bounding the LLM to local bound reasoning for non-deterministic outcomes, an observability-driven approach is used to achieve reduced context space spanning the IT stack and underlying app source code (if relevant) for incident root cause analysis (and other use cases). With this approach, leveraging the equivalent Instana data model, we have seen the proprietary Instana “I3” (intelligent incident investigation [8]) agent achieve up to 4.0× improvement over ReAct agent with GPT-5.1 as measured using ITBench [9]. With Gemini 3 Flash the ReAct agent performance improves to within 17% lower than the I3 agent while consuming 1.6× more tokens, We have extended this approach to source code with agents for code analysis (leveraging program dependency graphs) and bug remediation (leveraging inference scaling), also tested on ITBench, illustrating superior performance for the source code analysis and bug remediation agents (Gemini 2.5 Flash) over state-of-the-art coding agent both for finding the culpable microservice (3.0×) and bug repair (1.6×) while consuming respectively 3.7× and 5.9× less tokens. This multi-agent system was announced at IBM Think as part of the newly unveiled IBM Concert Platform for shift-left IT Operations and is also being piloted internally with IBM CIO. [10]

Enterprises face increasingly complex and fragmented compliance requirements, forcing teams to spend considerable time manually creating controls, assessments and remediation plans. No centralized knowledge exists and fixes are written manually, which introduces a risk of errors and security gaps. Because compliance work is complex and multi-step, it requires coordinated policy-driven automation across specialized agents rather than manual effort or simple AI prompts. Our multi-agent system automates compliance by algorithmically decomposing complex tasks into coordinated steps, using adaptive planning, dynamic decomposition and workflow sequencing with continuous feedback to iteratively identify fixes and expand assessments. It is 1.3 – 2.0× more performant than prior agents (Claude 4 Sonnet) using fixed planning strategies, as also measured using ITBench. This approach transforms compliance into a continuously guided self-correcting process and dramatically improves outcomes, especially in complex scenarios, boosting success rates from single digits to as high as +80% (Claude 4 Sonnet). This multi-agent system and 16K+ digitized controls mappings were unveiled as part of IBM Sovereign Core at IBM Think, integrated with monitoring, drift detection, providing automated evidence generation, ensuring audit evidence stays securely within customer control. [12]

The above examples illustrate the impact of agent logic in reducing LLM context and guiding the LLM to traverse the core of the workflow in a highly performant and cost-effective manner. Additionally, we have employed similar approaches to two case studies, one with a configurable generalist agent and runtime (CUGA) in the healthcare domain and another for the condition-based maintenance for physical assets with IBM Global Real Estate.

Case Study 1: Configurable Generalist Agent (CUGA) Healthcare benchmark - algorithmic policy enforcement. [13]

The following health insurance customer care example is a compact illustration of why agentic systems outperform LLM-only conversational models in regulated environments. CUGA’s (configurable generalist agent) policy system implements policy-as-code for agent governance, which is enforced at runtime independent of model prompts and without fine-tuning. Our experiments show that the agent’s policy system closes large gaps in task correctness, enforcing structured workflows, safe intent handling, reliable tool usage, and controlled output formatting across all model families (Claude Opus – 4.5, GPT OSS 120B and GPT – 4.1) with accuracy improvements ranging from 15% to 26%. Authority is enforced through least-privilege disclosure, explicit compliance rules, and human escalation paths. Intelligent actions are proposed, while authority is exercised by policy and oversight mechanisms. Reasoning is autonomous; decision rights are constrained. CUGA is also a key component in the IBM Think Sovereign Core launch.

Case Study 2: Condition-based Maintenance of Physical Assets for IBM Global Real Estate - directed acyclic graph. [14],[15]

Enterprise maintenance systems collect copious amounts of asset data but are unable to effectively combine them, demanding experts to manually piece together fragmented signals and make decisions without unified, evidence-based insights. Our recently launched Maximo Condition Insights [16] agent analyzes large-scale asset data across thousands of assets and locations (sensors, work orders, failure modes and events analysis), using structured evidence and validation loops to reliably identify issues, prioritize actions and support decision-making with consistent, traceable insights. We have piloted this agent (using GPT OSS 120B) internally with IBM Global Real Estate (GRE), reducing asset analysis time from 15-20 mins to 15-30 sec (a 97% improvement) and increasing asset review coverage from ~1% to ~30% spanning over 120 sites and 6K physical assets. Using AssetOpsBench, the Condition Insights agent reduced unsupported claims by 57%, cut verbosity by 35%, improved rule compliance by 30%, maintained near-zero contradictions, and lowered token usage by on average 77%, while slightly increasing diagnostic specificity. This agent, equipped with a directed acyclic graph, provides structural engineering and operational context to reduce unsupported reasoning under naive prompting, while constraint-aware prompting markedly improves rule adherence, reduces verbosity, and lowers overall token consumption without introducing instability.

Summary and References: We have benefited from guides for centuries, which have simplified and enhanced our lives. As technology has evolved, so have the guides we use, enabling us to do more and further shrink our global village. With the arrival of this agentic AI era, as we seek to further enhance society in part through economies of scale, we should continue this trend and fully leverage agent logic to simplify model context and intelligently traverse enterprise workflows at the core; only then will scalable adoption at optimal operating costs be truly feasible.

Nvidia today held its first all-hands meeting since the resignation of co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang. According to Wired, interim CEO Colette Kress offered more money and equity on a faster-than-expected schedule to calm staffers' nerves."So I’m here to tell you, the best thing that we want to do is to take care of each and every single employee that is here and to make sure that you feel good about this company and you do not worry about your comp,” Wired reports Kress said.The pay and equity bumps are set for December, far ahead of the company's normal raise cycle. Kress said that compensation and more clarity from the board were the most common topics in questions submitted ahead of the meeting. Keeping current employees happy will be one of Kress' most important short-term challenges. One director-level employee has already written to the board and top executives, warning that failure to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive could lead to the loss of ‘irreplaceable talent.’

A potential exodus of talent could also spook investors, despite standout earnings on Thursday. A leadership crisis could make the company seem less stable, and Huang had placed himself as the anchor point for many decisions and the company's overall vision.Huang has expressed interest in returning to Nvidia, saying he would be "honored" to lead the company again if asked by the board. The board was clear in yesterday's earnings call that it did not intend to bring Huang back, though there is reportedly a pro-Huang faction.Nvidia cofounder Chris Malachowsky was also on the call, explaining that the company lives its values rather than simply plastering them on posters.“We’re going to be fine,” he said.

#10159. Your SSL certificates can now last 200 days at most: The real risk isn’t renewal

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Every SSL certificate comes with a limited lifespan. Following the latest update from the CA/Browser Forum, the maximum lifetime of a certificate has fallen from 398 days to 200, and it will drop to 100 days in March 2027 and 47 days in 2029. Renewal is no longer an annual chore. It’s an ongoing task that only stays manageable with automation.

So what does this mean if you already look after sites with SSL certificates, and will it bring drastic changes? For many setups, very little will change. For others, one missed renewal can mean an outage. This article explains what’s changing and what to do if you’re in the second group.

Today, an SSL certificate is valid for 200 days at most. The limit applies when a certificate is issued, so the ones you already hold keep their original expiration date.

Where you feel it depends on how your certificates renew. Sites on managed hosting platforms or behind a content delivery network (CDN) usually renew automatically already, often every 90 days, so the new limit changes little. The pressure lands on setups where someone buys a certificate once a year and installs it by hand. At 47 days, that becomes about 12 renewals a year.

A certificate is a promise from a certificate authority that a key really belongs to a domain, and that promise gets less reliable the longer it runs. If a private key leaks, or a certificate is issued by mistake, it stays usable until it expires. Cutting the lifetime shrinks that window, so a problem that once lingered for over a year is now fixed in weeks.

Shorter lifetimes also make revocation, the process for canceling a bad certificate, far less critical. Revocation has never worked perfectly, but a certificate that expires within weeks matters much less if a cancellation doesn’t reach every browser.

Another reason is about people. A task done once a year is easy to forget and hard to check from outside. Browser makers have pushed for years to move the industry onto automatic renewal, on the logic that a process that runs every few weeks gets tested constantly. If it breaks, you notice quickly instead of discovering it on the day the certificate expires.

For most people, the first effect is simply more work. A certificate that once needed attention every year will soon need it every few weeks. Plus, each renewal is a small chance for something to go wrong. Multiply that by dozens of sites, mail servers, and devices, and the chance of one slipping through grows quickly.

The safety nets are also thinner. If you relied on the renewal emails, nothing is watching your certificates now. Additionally, with a shorter life, there’s less time between this should have renewed and this has expired.

An expired certificate doesn’t make a site slow or dated. It makes it unreachable for most visitors. Chrome, Firefox, and Safari all show a full-page warning that the connection isn’t private, and most people leave instead of clicking through. If the site uses HSTS, a setting that tells browsers to connect only over secure links, there is often no way to click through at all, and visitors are blocked outright until the certificate is fixed.

The damage doesn’t stop at the home page. Checkouts, contact forms, and logins that depend on the secure connection fail along with it, often without an error message that points at the real cause. Other systems break, too, because apps and integrations that call your site over a secure link refuse to connect to an expired certificate.

Nothing about your site has to change for any of this to happen. A date passes, and a site that worked on Friday is down on Monday. In a 47-day lifetime, that date comes around about every six weeks.

Automatic renewal tools do the heavy lifting well. The failures happen around them:

Look at the five failures above and you’ll see what they share. Each one happens quietly. The renewal job ran, or looked like it did, and nobody checked what the server was actually serving afterwards. Automation can tell you it tried. It can’t tell you the result reached your visitors.

What closes that gap is a check that never relies on your server’s own account of events. Site24x7’s SSL/TLS certificate monitoring does exactly that. It reads the certificate installed on your web server from the cloud, the way a visitor’s browser would, and alerts you before it expires, using thresholds you choose. If a renewal fails quietly, you hear about it from the monitor and not from a customer.

For each certificate, it records the issuing authority, the owner, the issue date, the expiration date, and the days remaining, including on servers that host several certificates behind one address. That last number matters more as lifespans shrink. When a certificate lasts 47 days, the days left is the figure that tells you a renewal is overdue, and you can set your warning against it using the quarter-of-the-lifetime rule covered next.

Once a monitor is watching your certificates, the next question is when it should speak up.

Most expiration alerts are set to a fixed number of days: warn at 30 days left and escalate at seven. That works for a certificate that lasts a year and renews with a month to spare. It breaks when the whole certificate lasts for a limited number of days.

Here’s why: a healthy certificate renews with about a third of its life still left. If your alert appears earlier than that, it goes off on certificates that are doing nothing wrong, and soon everyone ignores it. As lifespans shrink, a fixed 30-day alert will start doing exactly that.

The fix is to set the alerts based on lateness, not on how close the expiry date is. Warn when a quarter of the lifetime is left, since a renewal is overdue by then, and escalate when a tenth is left. Because these are shares of the lifetime, they keep working, however short lifespans get.

The next cut lands on March 15, 2027, so a few checks now will save you from scrambling later:

Shorter lifespans won’t break your site, but a missed renewal will, so fix the quiet failures now while a mistake still costs an afternoon to fix, not a Monday morning outage affecting lots of customers.

If you’d like a second pair of eyes on your certificates, you can start a 30-day free trial of Site24x7’s SSL/TLS certificate monitoring.

Now that Apple’s foldable is here, Google wants to make sure apps on Android foldables are a good experience. Starting in April 2027, Google is going to require Android developers to make sure their apps have a baseline level of support for foldables. If they don’t, developers risk not being able to publish or update their apps or have reduced visibility for their apps on Google Play.

Google says Android apps must meet its “Tier 3 — Adaptive ready” standard. “Apps must fill the available display area without letterboxing or compatibility modes,” Google says. “Apps must preserve state (scroll position, text input, media playback) during rotation, folding/unfolding, and resizing, while supporting multi-window environments.” (The other two tiers are “Adaptive optimized” and “Adaptive differentiated” and take further advantage of the possibilities of foldables.) As of the April 2027 deadline, developers also will have to include three foldable screenshots for their app listings. Developers can start publishing their foldable screenshots today.

Similar requirements will apply to games, though developers have until August 2027 to get their titles ready for Android foldables, Google says. (Google “plans to extend” its requirements to other large-screen devices like tablets and Googlebook laptops in “future phases.”) However, game developers will still need to share three foldable screenshots for app listings starting in April.

The changes are being announced just weeks after Apple launched the iPhone Duo, which already has more than 200,000 optimized apps, though some developers are still figuring out Apple’s foldable form factor.

#10156. Introducing Mellum2: A 12B Mixture-of-Experts Model by JetBrains

Today we’re releasing Mellum2, an open Mixture-of-Experts model optimized for low-latency text-and-code workloads. Mellum originally started as a code completion model. With Mellum2, we extend that foundation to a broader set of natural language and software engineering tasks while keeping the model focused on efficient inference and deployability. Modern AI systems increasingly rely on multiple model calls: routing, retrieval, summarization, planning, validation, and tool use. Many of these operations are latency-sensitive and do not require the largest available model. Mellum2 targets these workloads.

In our technical report, we evaluate Mellum2 across code generation, reasoning, science, and math benchmarks. Mellum2 is competitive with similarly sized open models while delivering more than 2x faster inference, making it suitable for high-throughput production workloads. Model architecture Mellum2 is a Mixture-of-Experts model:

The MoE architecture keeps total model capacity high while activating only a subset of parameters for each token. This makes inference more efficient and helps reduce serving cost for real-time workloads. Mellum2 is intentionally focused on text and code rather than multimodal tasks. This specialization keeps the model compact and efficient for software engineering workloads.

Mellum2 works well as a lightweight routing and orchestration model in multi-model systems, including prompt classification, tool selection, and intermediate control-flow steps.

The model is well suited for latency-sensitive retrieval pipelines, including context compression, summarization, and retrieval post-processing.

Mellum2 can be used for agent subtasks such as planning, validation, transformation, and context preparation, reducing the need to invoke larger models for intermediate operations.

Because Mellum2 is open and efficient to serve, it can be deployed in self-hosted environments involving proprietary code or internal data.

As AI systems mature, the most effective architectures are becoming less monolithic. A single frontier model can be powerful, but production systems often need several specialized components working together: retrievers, routers, code-aware models, validators, tool callers, and larger reasoning models. We think of Mellum2 as a “focal” model: a fast, well-scoped model optimized for high-frequency tasks inside larger AI systems. The goal is not to replace every model in the stack. The goal is to make the stack faster, cheaper, and easier to control.

If you are building AI systems for software engineering – inside an IDE, in a RAG pipeline, as part of an agent workflow, or on private infrastructure – Mellum2 is ready to try.

That would use up to 5% of a typical 1TB SSD’s rated endurance each year.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nvidia’s GeForce driver 621.14 is reportedly causing excessive background writes on idle PCs, inducing extra wear on SSDs. One user measured about 3GB an hour on the susceptible driver, and another mentioned estimated up to 30GB/hour on the newer 621.24. This follows a similar-looking bug from AMD’s video driver discovered last month.

The bug is described by user Andergraude in an Nvidia forum post as “new in 621.14,” which came out on Nov. 4, who says it operates by “continuously [rewriting] the binary log file” with “real writes” to the drive. The writes are coming from the NVDisplay.Container.exe process, or the “NVIDIA Display Container LS” service, which logs to the nvlog.nvlgstg file. This background service is necessary for running the Nvidia Control Panel and App. It’s not clear what’s written in the log, and not every system is necessarily impacted.

The “real writes” point comes from the fact that a per-process write counter is not the same as writes reaching the drive. The measurements came from Windows Resource Monitor, Windows performance counters, and CrystalDiskInfo. The Data Units Written counter matched Windows’ reporting. This test showed 515MB of process I/O coming with 270MB of total writes to the C: drive over five minutes. That works out to roughly 3GB per hour, in line with the user’s own estimate.

Worse, “the write volume increases as the file grows.” Stopping the service and deleting the log can temporarily reduce the writes. With the previous driver version 621.01, the writes totaled less than 2MB per five minutes, and a second user in the thread confirmed that a rollback helps.

Mitigation attempts, such as three clean reinstalls with the help of DDU from that second user, did not fix the problem. The writing process also impacted gaming and video performance, potentially causing hitching, which suggests it gets worse under load.

Another user, AyzekUorren, in a separate thread about driver 621.24, which came out Nov. 12, says that it could get up to “about 30gb per 1h” or even “70gb or even more” with longer sessions. This is even with telemetry disabled in the Nvidia App. Noted is that every Alt+Tab added 500MB to 1GB of writes, at least for this user.

In AMD’s case, it was the External Events Utility, or atieclxx.exe, that exhibited constant writes on an idle PC. In that case, the AMD utility was reportedly copying its own executable every second. To put the impact into context, the AMD bug had rates reported between 0.3 and 5MB/s while total drive writes in the 621.14 test measured around 0.9MB/s.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The Nvidia numbers are somewhat alarming, given that a typical 1TB SSD is rated for 600TB of writes over a standard five-year warranty. Even at 270MB per five minutes, this could be about 28TB per year — for a never-sleeping PC — which is reaching toward 5% of the drive’s rated endurance, although the writes include everything the system is writing and realistic uptime will be less. However, at the higher end — 30GB per hour, at eight hours a day — one could see 15% of drive endurance worn every year for nothing.

This doesn’t make it a drive killer, but given how much users value drive endurance, especially with SSD prices as they are, avoiding unnecessary writes like this is certainly a priority. To see if you’re affected, check Resource Monitor and look for the telltale NVDisplay.Container.exe and the nvlog.nvlgstg file in the list. You can also check the SMART Data Units Written value with CrystalDiskInfo or equivalent, such as your drive’s SSD toolbox.

At this time, no fix or hotfix has been announced, and the best workaround is to do a rollback. A similar issue in the past, fixed with driver update 471.96 back in 2021, was covered by Nvidia’s release notes. As it stands, Nvidia has “N/A” for 621.24’s Open Issues, and the company has not acknowledged the bug. For the AMD bug, the driver wasn't fixed for over three weeks (and came as an optional update).

#10154. Fitbit Edge after 30 days: Life in the middle lane [Video]

The biggest compliment you can pay Google at the moment is that alongside the Pixel Watch, recent Fitbit releases have been a huge return to form – the Fitbit Edge included.

I need to nail my colors to the mast; I’m a Fitbit Air fanboy. I’ve talked about it multiple times on the Pixelated podcast, here on the site, and it made me switch away from the Pixel Watch 5 because of how easily it fit into my existence without insisting on itself.

The Fitbit Edge worried me at first because it comes with a screen, which is something I realized isn’t that important to me day-to-day. After 30 days of wear, I’m conflicted because maybe I was too hasty to ditch a display on my wrist.

The design is somewhat in a halfway house because it feels like it’s trying to be both a classic Fitbit while integrating some of the Pixel Watch features we know and love. Initially, I loved it, but it has become something that isn’t quite enough in either direction to suit my own tastes.

My love for the simplicity of the Fitbit Air has colored how I feel, but the Edge has an excellent core design. The display bezels remind me heavily of the original Pixel Watch; yes, they’re there, but you only notice them when the light catches the frame edge.

After a month of daily wear, the display has lost a bit of its luster. The oleophobic coating is just about holding up, but now we’re into the cooler months; it’ll be put through a barrage of jacket cuffs and hoodie sleeves. This is one of the only durability concerns I have had so far.

Despite that admittedly minor concern, the Fitbit Edge is not something you need to baby. I’ve bashed it with weights, caught my wrist on zips (zippers for you, my American friends), and bashed it around with reckless abandon. It’s solid and hasn’t picked up as much as a single scuff. I don’t care too much if a fitness tracker gets a beating, whereas I would be more concerned about damaging my Pixel Watch.

If you come in wanting a smartwatch-like experience from the Fitbit Edge, I think you’ll instantly be frustrated by the UI. It can feel cramped when you see notifications, and the large bezels don’t help all that much, but Google has well optimized almost all of the key sections outside of this.

Tiles are very well implemented; they’re just a smaller, squatter take on the Pixel Watch tile system, and it’s one of the best things about the Fitbit Edge interface. It’s also really snappy, which is something that isn’t the case with cheaper fitness trackers such as this. I’m constantly checking the weather or using the Google Health tile, but I have loved the quick access complication on the default watch face.

I tried a few of the other designs over the past 30 days; a lot of them are great. The default has become my favorite. It’s information-dense without being too overloaded. Tapping the complications takes you to the exact data point. I genuinely love how fuss-free an experience it is, save for a few minor complaints.

We could criticize the accuracy of the data or the lack of tracking for certain types of workouts, but I think that misses the point of the Fitbit Edge. It’s a simple tracker with a screen, and the fact that you get even basic ECG on a device of this size is impressive.

I truly have worn the Edge daily for a full month, and while the bands are comfortable, I have found that they cause me to get a rash on the underside of my left wrist just under the palm. It’s actively stopping me from wearing it all the time now. I hope that the new connector doesn’t slow down third-party development for bands, because I’m desperate for a fabric band to alleviate this issue.

This is exacerbated when the rubber band gets wet or sweaty. If you have sensitive skin, you might have the same problem as I have. Using some moisturizer has helped, but it is something I wasn’t prepared to suffer with before the Fitbit Edge turned up. I get that this is likely a “me” problem, but I wanted to note it.

When the screen gets wet or moist, it can bug out quite a lot. Taps don’t register properly, and a few water droplets can activate all the menus and submenus. Luckily, it won’t force your phone to place a call or anything like that, but the water protection mode is a must. I have kept it on extensively.

Swimmers will probably get super frustrated; heck, I was on a rainy day as the screen kept bugging out. Overall, though, I have enjoyed the fitness tracking. Unlike on the Fitbit Air, it is nice to have a screen to start a workout rather than head over to my phone. That said, the experience is the same as on your phone, but scaled down to fit the watch face.

I dislike that you don’t get a phone notification to show the current workout progress by default, like the Fitbit Air. I had become accustomed to that. Luckily, you can enable it in the Google Health settings. I like having this as I forget to stop workouts so often without a prompt to hit “stop.”

With audio playback, you’re also getting the partial benefits of watch-phone controls, but it’s a two-step process unlike on Pixel Watch. You either have to go to the “Media” app or have the tile active and navigate to it to access play/pause and all your other streaming app controls. I tend not to bother using these as it’s finicky.

This had me thinking about NFC. I think a lot of people would have liked NFC for Google Wallet on the Fitbit Edge, but I think having to enter a PIN on such a small screen would really have been a nightmare. I’ve made wireless payments with my watch less than five times, as it’s just easier to use my phone rather than contort my wrist to a wireless payment terminal. I figure this was something that was thought about and makes a lot of sense given the constraints.

One of my other complaints is that the DND and Bedtime modes from my account haven’t synced or at least don’t appear to sync. Unless I’m mistaken, you need to activate these settings manually every time, which has been super annoying when in bed, as a flick of your wrist can blind you in a dark room. I figure this is something that can be fixed with an update, so here’s hoping.

I’ve been super impressed with the battery life. A week is easily attainable for me with up to three gym visits per week, so I’ve charged 5 times in a month. That, to me, is excellent. I picked up a cheap charging dock, as the Edge uses the same charger for the Fitbit Air, so I figured why not.

It’s not the best-looking dock, but I quite like how it airs off my Edge so it’s not as stinky after gym sessions – as I wipe with an alcohol pad and clean as regularly as possible.

The experience is fine; it’s almost a third of the price of the Pixel Watch and lacks a few features due to the various compromises – compromises I can deal with, as smartwatches have become information overload for me over time, and I like that the app selection is ultra-refined. At no point does the Fitbit Edge give you information overload.

Coming from a Charge 6 or an older Fitbit, this is an amazing replacement. It’s the new “default” fitness tracker for people who want all the hallmarks of what makes a great Fitbit.

There is just enough. Nothing more, nothing less. To me, this feels like the perfect middle ground for a lot of people. You want something simple, touchscreen-enabled, and that doesn’t get in the way. As impressed as I have been with the Edge, though, I’ve loved a fuss-free tech accessory so much recently that I’ll probably go back to the Fitbit Air.

#10153. Holo3.1: Fast & Local Computer Use Agents

Last March, we released Holo3, our state-of-the-art computer-use model. Adoption was immediate. Developers, enterprises, and partners started deploying Holo3 across a wide range of workflows, from browser automation and business software to internal tools and desktop applications. As adoption grew, we realized performance alone was no longer enough.

Users want to run the same computer-use capabilities across desktop and mobile environments, with seamless integration with different agent frameworks. They want deployment flexibility, from cloud inference to fully local execution on end-user devices.

This is why we are releasing the Holo3.1 family. Holo3.1 improves robustness across the three dimensions that matter most in production: environments (web, desktop, mobile), agent frameworks, and deployment targets. For the first time, we release quantized checkpoints optimized for local inference, including FP8, Q4 GGUF, and NVFP4.

Holo3.1 is a major step toward our vision of universal computer-use agents: systems that can operate across environments, integrate into any agent stack, and run wherever the workflow lives.

Based on the Qwen family, Holo3.1 was designed to improve robustness across the environments where computer-use agents are actually deployed, while retaining state-of-the-art performance.

As teams moved Holo3 from evaluation to production, we repeatedly observed the same challenge: strong performance in one setting does not necessarily transfer to another. Mobile devices, alternative agent harnesses, and different execution frameworks all introduce their own sources of distribution shift.

Holo3.1 expands Holo3's capabilities beyond browser and desktop control, delivering major gains on mobile environments. On AndroidWorld, our 35B-A3B model improves from 67% to 79.3%, while the smaller 4B and 9B variants improve from 58% to 72%.

To better support teams deploying Holo inside third-party agent stacks, Holo3.1 introduces native support for function-calling protocols in addition to the structured JSON outputs already available in Holo3.

Across OSWorld and our internal benchmark suite covering e-commerce, business software, and collaboration workflows, function-calling and native execution now achieve near-parity performance. Holo3.1 also delivers more than a 25% improvement over Holo3 when evaluated inside our Holotab product harness.

To further enable local and on-device inference, we are also releasing new model sizes including small models (0.8B, 4B, and 9B) for cost-effective and private deployment, in addition to the larger 35B-A3B model for state-of-the-art performance.

Performance versus cost for the Holo3.1 and Qwen 3.5 families. Overall performance averages the four H Corporate benchmarks first (so each family is equally weighted), then takes the mean across OSWorld, AndroidWorld, H Corporate, ScreenSpot-Pro, and OSWorld-G.

This is our first release to ship quantized weights. We’re starting with 35B-A3B checkpoints, available in FP8, Q4 GGUF, and NVFP4.

For NVFP4, we used NVIDIA's Model Optimizer in a W4A16 configuration. These checkpoints enable fast local inference for Computer Use Agents with little to no degradation in model performance. FP8 and NVFP4 achieve the same OSWorld scores, only about two points below the full-precision BF16 checkpoint.

The speedups are substantial: on DGX Spark, NVFP4 W4A16 delivers 1.41× the total token throughput of FP8 and 1.74× that of BF16.

We also release Q4 GGUF checkpoints aimed at local deployment of Computer Use Agents on consumer hardware.

The agent itself runs locally on a Windows or Mac machine, while the model can either run on that same machine—we include reference numbers for Apple Silicon—or on a DGX Spark on the same network. In both cases, execution stays fully private and local, with nothing leaving the user's network.

On Spark, agent harness optimizations we developed with NVIDIA combined with the NVFP4 quantization above deliver a compound ~2× end-to-end speedup over the FP8 baseline, cutting average step time from 6.8s to 3.3s.

Agent request rate across platforms and precisions. On DGX Spark, vLLM with NVFP4 achieves the highest request rate in both Default and Fast modes, followed by Q4 GGUF and FP8. These improvements and more will land in an upcoming desktop agent harness.

The Holo3.1 family is available in four sizes:

We are also releasing optimized FP8, NVFP4, and Q4 GGUF checkpoints for local and edge deployment.

We look forward to seeing what developers build with Holo3.1.

With Grand Theft Auto VI set to finally launch tomorrow, November 19th, our long-awaited return to Vice City is nearly here. But after all this time, some of the gear you’ve used in San Andreas might feel out of place on the glamorous streets of Leonidas County. Luckily for you, we’ve gathered a few of our favorite Xbox and PlayStation 5 accessories to help your long gaming sessions run as smoothly as possible.

The 8BitDo Ultimate 3E — an upgraded pick for Xbox Series X and Series S consoles — is a very capable, comfortable controller with elite-level features, including a high polling rate and adjustable triggers. It’s on the expensive side at $149.99, but the customization and clean execution justify the cost. Read our review.

PlayStation 5 owners looking for a controller upgrade, meanwhile, might consider the DualSense Edge, Sony’s first-party pro-style controller. In addition to a variety of extra function buttons and paddles, the wireless gamepad sports adjustable trigger heights and swappable joysticks (in case the potentiometers start to drift). It’s a little bit heavier than Sony’s regular DualSense, and the battery life isn’t quite as good, but it offers customization you won’t find on the console’s default controller. Read our review.

Sony’s pro-style controller, the DualSense Edge, might suffer from shorter battery life than the standard DualSense model, but it features great software integration with the PlayStation 5 and plenty of customizable components.

Nothing’s worse than having to pause a heist so you can go hunt down a fresh set of AA batteries. The PowerA Duo Charging Station includes a rechargeable battery and replacement rear doors for two Xbox Series X / S or Xbox One controllers. Simply set them on the dock, and they’ll start charging.

PowerA’s PlayStation equivalent charges two DualSense Wireless Controllers simultaneously, with an included AC adapter, and comes with a two-year warranty.

The 2026 Roku Pro Series is the brand’s first OLED, and the 55-inch version retails for $999.99, which is on the low end of the price spectrum for OLED. Games feel richer and more immersive on OLED panels, thanks to their deeper black levels, which are the result of unlit pixels or sections of the screen. Each Pro Series panel also sports a 120Hz refresh rate, four HDMI 2.1 ports, and both low latency and variable refresh rates for gaming.

For a more premium offering, the Sony Bravia 8 II is one of our favorite screens for movies, with an engaging, immersive picture and excellent image processing. It has great gaming features, too, like a 120Hz refresh rate with variable refresh and an automatic low-latency mode. It’s not cheap, but the OLED makes for an excellent upgrade to your setup. Read our review.

Sony’s latest first-party headset, the $99 PlayStation Pulse Wireless, launches the same day as GTA VI. My colleague Cameron Faulkner recently went hands-on with the wireless headset ahead of its launch on November 19th, and came away impressed with its overall audio quality and comfort. The newest Pulse is also straightforward to set up and use, especially when paired with devices like the PlayStation Portal that support PlayStation Link, Sony’s proprietary low-latency audio connection. It also offers Bluetooth for use with other devices.

For Xbox gamers, it’s hard to beat the SteelSeries Arctis Nova 3X, which retails in multiple colors for $109.99 or less. The wireless headset is lightweight, comfortable, and compatible with a wide variety of other consoles and mobile devices as well, for those rare moments when you aren’t playing GTA VI.

If you’d rather the simplicity of a wired option, Sony’s InZone H6 Air skips the batteries and dongles, instead opting to plug straight into your controller. This open-back gaming headset is lightweight and comfortable, which is great for long hours and late nights. My colleague Cameron Faulkner described its sound as “spectacular,” with several equalizer options available for helping fine-tune the sound to your liking. Read our review.

Ikea’s Poäng chair balances affordability and comfort, with wide, supportive armrests that are just the right height for holding a controller. It comes in a variety of frame materials and cushion colors, too, making it easy to match your other furniture or console. This is my personal chair for console gaming, and I recently added a matching ottoman to the set for maximum relaxation.

#10151. Logging AI Prompts and Responses in Java Without Leaking Sensitive Data

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Picture this. A customer writes to your support chatbot: "Hi, I'm Asha, my card ending 4111 was charged twice, call me on 98400 12345." Your Java service wraps that message in a prompt, sends it to a model, and logs the whole thing so you can debug it later. Congratulations, you now have a customer's name, phone number and card details sitting in a plain text log file that half the engineering team can open.

This happens more often than people admit. Logging AI calls is genuinely useful, but prompts and responses are some of the most personal text your application ever touches. Here's how to keep the usefulness and drop the risk.

A regular web request is easy to log: URL, status code, time taken. AI calls are messier.

The output changes from run to run. If a user says "your bot gave me a wrong answer yesterday", the only proof of what happened is what you sent and what came back at that moment. You can't just replay it and expect the same result.

Prompts are also built, not typed. The final text is usually a template, a few retrieved document chunks, some chat history and the user's message stitched together. When something looks off, the bug could be in any of those pieces, and only the assembled prompt shows you which one.

Then there's cost. You pay by the token, so without per-call records you can't say which feature is burning money. And quality drifts over time as models get upgraded and templates get edited. Old logs are your only baseline.

So yes, you need these logs. The real question is what goes into them.

Before writing any masking code, agree on what counts as sensitive. In most business apps that means:

Names, emails, phone numbers and home addresses

Card numbers, bank details and government ID numbers

Health, legal or job-related details people mention in free text

Internal material like contract wording, pricing rules or source code

The first three groups follow patterns, so they're easy to catch. The last two don't, and that's where most teams get caught out. Keep that in mind, because it shapes the design below.

The safest sensitive value is the one that never reaches the log. So split what you record into two buckets.

The first is metadata: a request ID, a hashed user or tenant ID, model name, prompt template name and version, token counts, latency, retry count, error type and estimated cost. None of this is personal, and it answers most day-to-day questions.

The second is content, meaning the actual prompt and response text. You only need this when you're investigating quality, and even then you rarely need all of it. A sensible default is to log metadata for every call and masked content for a small sample, maybe five percent, plus every failed call.

Here's a mistake that's easy to make: letting the log appender clean things up afterwards. By then the raw text may already be in a buffer, an async queue or a crash dump. Mask first, then log.

The cleanest way is one small component that every AI log call has to pass through:

public interface PiiMasker {     String mask(String input); }

Nothing else is allowed to write raw prompts. One chokepoint is much easier to review and test than masking sprinkled across fifty classes.

For structured data like emails, cards and tokens, regular expressions do the job well:

public class RegexPiiMasker implements PiiMasker {     private static final Map RULES = new LinkedHashMap<>();     static {         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("[A-Za-z0-9.%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}"), "[EMAIL]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,19}\b"), "[CARD]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("\b(?:\+?\d{1,3}[ -]?)?\d{10}\b"), "[PHONE]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("(?i)bearer\s+[A-Za-z0-9.~+/=-]+"), "Bearer [TOKEN]");     }     @Override     public String mask(String input) {         if (input == null || input.isBlank()) return input;         String result = input;         for (var rule : RULES.entrySet()) {             result = rule.getKey().matcher(result).replaceAll(rule.getValue());         }         return result;     } }

A few small choices matter here. The patterns are compiled once, not on every call. The order is fixed, because a card number can otherwise get half eaten by the phone rule. And the replacement labels such as [EMAIL] keep the sentence readable, so whoever debugs it later can still follow what the user was asking.

Regex won't catch a name like "Asha Raman" or an address buried mid-sentence. For those you have a few options, and they work best together.

You can run a named-entity recognition model that tags people, places and organisations, then mask anything above a confidence threshold. You can do exact replacement of values you already know, such as the customer's name from the current session. Or, best of all, you can mask at the field level while building the prompt. If your code knows that customer.getEmail() is going into the template, swap in a placeholder right there instead of trying to spot it afterwards. Knowing beats guessing every time.

Plain redaction can remove too much. If the same email shows up five times in a conversation, five identical [EMAIL] tags hide the fact that it was one person.

The fix is consistent pseudonyms. Turn each real value into a short token using a keyed hash, so the same email always becomes something like EMAIL_7f3a. You can still follow the thread, but nobody can read the original from the log. Use an HMAC with a secret from your secrets manager. A plain unkeyed hash of a phone number can be brute-forced in minutes, because there just aren't that many phone numbers.

One warning: if you also store a lookup table to reverse the tokens, that table is now sensitive data too. Most teams are better off with one-way tokens.

Free-text log lines are hard to search and easy to leak through. Write one JSON record per AI call with clearly separate fields:

log.info("ai_call",     kv("requestId", requestId),     kv("model", model),     kv("promptVersion", "support-reply-v4"),     kv("inputTokens", usage.inputTokens()),     kv("outputTokens", usage.outputTokens()),     kv("latencyMs", elapsed),     kv("promptMasked", masker.mask(prompt)),     kv("responseMasked", masker.mask(response)));

Now dashboards for cost and latency never need to touch the text fields at all. You can also keep the two kinds of data for different lengths of time: metadata for a year, masked content for a couple of weeks. Put the request ID into your logging framework's MDC so every line belonging to one call, including retries and tool calls, carries the same ID.

Streaming trips people up. Tokens arrive in tiny pieces, and a card number can be split across two chunks, which means masking each chunk on its own will miss it. Collect the full response in a buffer, mask it once the stream ends, and log that. If the stream dies halfway, run the partial buffer through the same masker.

Tool calls are the other trap. When the model calls one of your Java methods, the arguments and return values are often the most sensitive thing in the whole exchange: order details, account balances, addresses. Treat them as part of the prompt and response. Log the tool name, duration and outcome by default, and log arguments only after masking.

Masking lowers the risk but never removes it, so surround it with some ordinary discipline:

Give content fields a short retention period. Old prompt archives are liabilities.

Limit who can read AI logs. Debugging a model doesn't mean someone needs to read customer messages.

Encrypt log storage and the pipeline that feeds it.

Log the hashed user ID so you can find and delete one person's records when they ask.

Allow verbose logging in development with fake data, and enforce strict settings in production through configuration, not through people remembering.

A masker that quietly stops working is worse than having none, because everyone assumes the logs are clean. Write tests for it:

@Test void masksEmailAndCardNumber() {     String raw = "Contact me at asha@example.com, card 4111 1111 1111 1111";     String safe = new RegexPiiMasker().mask(raw);     assertFalse(safe.contains("asha@example.com"));     assertFalse(safe.contains("4111"));     assertTrue(safe.contains("[EMAIL]"));     assertTrue(safe.contains("[CARD]")); }

Build a small set of messy, realistic samples: numbers with odd spacing, mixed languages, addresses inside sentences, text pasted from spreadsheets. Run them in your CI pipeline, and add a new case every time a leak turns up. A scheduled job that scans stored logs for patterns that should never appear makes a good safety net too.

A few I'd watch for. Logging raw text at debug level and assuming production never enables it; debug flags get switched on during incidents, so mask at every level. Masking only the user's message while forgetting retrieved documents, system prompts and tool results. Letting SDK exceptions carry the full request body into the logs. Leaving wire-level HTTP logging on in production, which bypasses your masker completely. And treating masking as finished once it ships, when every new prompt template can bring new kinds of data.

Every AI call writes a structured metadata record with a request ID

All prompt and response text goes through a single masker first

Streams are masked after assembly, and tool arguments are masked too

Content logging is sampled, short-lived and access-controlled

Tests cover the masker, with a regression case for every past leak

Client libraries aren't dumping raw payloads into the logs

Good logs turn an AI feature from a black box into something you can actually debug, price and improve. The same logs can also expose the people who trusted you with their details. The way through is fairly plain: record metadata for every call, push all content through one well-tested masker, use pseudonyms when you need to follow a conversation, handle streams and tools carefully, and keep retention short. Set that up before launch, not after the first incident, and you get visibility without regret.

#10150. Vivo X500 Pro camera review: Battle of the small(er) phones vs Pixel 11 Pro

The compact Vivo X500 Pro has some camera downgrades compared to the Pro Max, so are you better off saving money and getting the base Vivo X500 instead?

Over the past few years, Vivo has made a name for itself as the camera powerhouse smartphone company. The first time I used a Vivo X100 Pro blew my mind in a way smartphone cameras hadn’t for a few years, but does the company’s 4th iteration — yes, Vivo skipped the X400 — of the X series still impress?

The answer is mostly yes. The Vivo X500 series includes five models: the base X500, the X500 Pro, and the X500 Pro Max. Unlike some other phones, all three of these models feature different camera hardware that takes advantage of the physical size differences. The X500 Pro Max’s hardware is the best of the bunch, but that phone is substantially larger and heavier as a result.

So I’m comparing the more reasonably sized models to see which semi-compact Vivo phone you should consider this year. I tossed the Google Pixel 11 Pro into the comparison since Google also offers a compact flagship camera phone.

Most camera specs between these phones are surprisingly comparable, so the differences you’re about to see are largely caused by some pretty massive differences in processing. I already covered Vivo’s wild new AI camera mode, so let’s go for something a little closer to normal smartphone camera use: a day at the Biltmore.

Perhaps the biggest difference between these phones is Vivo’s pursuit of “perfection,” while Google seems to embrace a more “natural” look. At 10x and 5x, the photos from both Vivo phones are essentially noise-free, have clear sharpening applied to them, and are generally quite vibrant. Despite having similar specs, the Vivo X500 Pro’s more advanced Sony LYT telephoto sensor pulls out more detail.

Google’s images are notably softer, although not in a low-resolution sort of way. They look more like they’re taken from a standard camera rather than a smartphone, which some people may prefer. While telephoto image quality between the Vivo X500 Pro and Google Pixel 11 Pro is mostly down to preference, Google’s phone is substantially faster while taking the actual photo. In all of the darker shots, the Pixel 11 Pro took the picture instantly. Both Vivo X500 models took a 2-3 second exposure shot, making me stand there for longer than I’m used to.

Ultrawide performance is where I feel we see the largest gap between these phones. Both the Vivo X500 and X500 Pro cameras offer bright, well-balanced shots that are vibrant but not unrealistic. The light sources in the room emit a lovely warm glow, yet the bulbs themselves aren’t overblown. The X500 Pro’s slightly warmer image across all three scenarios looks best to me.

The Pixel 11 Pro’s ultrawide images are often underexposed and lacking in dynamic range. The staircase shot exhibits this problem the most. This can come off as natural in some scenarios, as modern smartphone photography is notorious for brightening dark areas too much, but too often the Pixel 11 Pro’s ultrawide shots just feel unnaturally dark.

The main camera is much more balanced, although it’s fun to push these phones to find their weaknesses. One of the best examples of differing priorities is in the wreath shot, which was quite dark in real life thanks to the bright sunlight outside. The Pixel 11 Pro valiantly tried to brighten up the shadows so you could actually see the wreath (since it’s clearly the subject), causing the rest of the scene to look forcefully bright.

The same issue cropped up in the image of the wine rack, where both Vivo phones captured a nicer-looking shot. The image of the trellis walkway is a tie, but the photo of my ridiculous bowl of ice cream looks best on the Vivo X500 Pro, once again.

Portrait mode is where I think the Vivo X500 Pro is the clear loser, but it’s not for any of the reasons in the other categories above. Rather, the X500 Pro seems to have some weird warping happening in the bokeh processing that’s not present on the base Vivo X500. This is in both front-facing and rear camera portrait shots, so it’s not a lens issue or some weird setting.

Google cleaned up its portrait shots so much this year that it’s borderline ridiculous. Pixels had the worst portrait mode for years, but this year’s overhaul of the portrait algorithm made all the difference in the world.

Overall, the Vivo X500 series is another solid release for Vivo, and while neither the base nor Pro models offer the same top-tier camera specs as the Pro Max model, it’s clear Vivo pulled off something great. The Vivo X500 Pro retails for €1,399 in the EU, while the base X500 global model is a little harder to find, but should be quite a bit cheaper if you can get your hands on it.

Quoting a Tom's Hardware post on the X social network discussing CEO Dr. Lisa Su meeting gamers and autographing a GPU, the AMD Japan account was quick to seize the moment. #10148. Adding MCP Tools to Reachy Mini

The Reachy Mini conversation app can now use tools hosted in public Hugging Face Spaces, called over MCP. You can give your robot a new ability, like checking the weather or searching the web, by adding a Space from the Hub instead of editing the app. The tool keeps running in the Space itself, so no code is downloaded onto your machine. And you can publish your own tools for other people to use.

Below, we look at what a tool is, how profiles control what the robot can use, and the current limits of the remote path.

When you talk to the robot, what you get back isn't only a voice, it's a system that reacts to the conversation: the robot can move and respond non-verbally, when it's applicable. The part we want to focus on here is the tools that make that possible. A tool is something the model can do during a conversation: play an emotion, move the head, look through the camera. Each tool has a name and a short description. The model reads those, decides when one is useful, calls it, and uses what comes back.

Today every tool is local and ships inside the app, and most of them are about the robot's body:

A tool in the code isn't usable until it's enabled in a profile, a folder with two files that matter here: instructions.txt (the prompt) and tools.txt (the tools that are turned on).

The default profile enables the full set:

If a name isn't in tools.txt, the model can't call it.

You can also write your own tool: add a Python file to the profile (or external_tools/), give it a name and description, and list that name in tools.txt.

Today there are built-in tools and custom local tools, and tools.txt decides which are active. This works well for the robot's body and keeps the trusted core small.

The constraint here is that every tool has to be local Python. For move_head or play_emotion that's right: they talk to the hardware and belong in the app but a lot of useful things have nothing to do with the body, like web search, weather, or lookups. For those, keeping everything local is mostly friction:

Remote tools add a third kind, alongside the built-in and custom local tools you already have, for capabilities that are easier to publish, share, and update on their own:

We started with two canary tools, small test tools to exercise the new flow:

They're enough to exercise the whole feature: install from the Hub, discover the remote tools, enable them per profile, and let the realtime backend call them exactly like built-in tools.

To use both at once, add each Space and their tools stack in the same profile:

Now the robot can search the web and check the weather in the same conversation, which is exactly what the canary_web_search_weather profile below does.

add validates the Space on the Hub, probes the MCP endpoint, discovers its tools, and by default appends the tool IDs to the active profile's tools.txt. The active profile is default unless you've set REACHY_MINI_CUSTOM_PROFILE. Use --install-only to skip that step.

tools.txt is the gatekeeper: a remote tool is only active if its ID appears in the profile's tools.txt, alongside whatever built-in tools you want.

Each installed Space gets a local alias derived from its slug, with hyphens, dots, and slashes collapsing to underscores:

Remote tools are then namespaced with a double underscore:

This keeps remote tool names from colliding with built-in ones and lets multiple Spaces coexist in the same profile.

The implementation also strips redundant Space-name prefixes when possible, so a verbose remote tool name becomes a cleaner local ID. If stripping would cause a collision between two tools from the same Space, the code falls back to the fully namespaced name.

There is also a duplicate safety check at registry level: Tool.name values must be unique across the entire merged tool set. The app fails fast if two sources claim the same name.

For this work we created two focused canary profiles to isolate the MCP experiment from the full embodied tool set.

The first keeps a few expressive tools (emotions, head movement) and adds web search on top:

The second is the same, plus the weather tool alongside search:

The small physical tool set means Reachy Mini can still react expressively while answering current questions from the web.

The remote-tool plumbing gets the tools into the model. The prompts decide how the model uses them.

That was especially visible in the search-plus-weather canary. A combined question like:

can be handled in at least three ways: weather first then search, search first then weather, or both in the same turn. If the prompt is vague, the model serialises the calls and creates unnecessary latency. So the canary prompts became part of the feature, not just incidental configuration.

Two things are worth calling out. First, the Space has to actually behave like an MCP server; if tool discovery fails, the install fails. Second, prompt instructions can encourage parallel calls but cannot guarantee them. If deterministic orchestration matters for a use case, that logic should move from the prompt into code.

If you want others to use your tool, publish it as a public Gradio Space that exposes the standard MCP endpoint, and keep the tools stateless so they work well over the network. Whether a Space installs depends on this runtime behavior, not on tags.

Tags aren't required for installation, but they help people find compatible Spaces:

The app now has three kinds of tools sharing one registry: built-in, local custom, and remote MCP tools, and profiles still decide which of them a given assistant can reach. A small, trusted core stays at the center while the optional capabilities around it can be added, tested, and swapped without touching the app itself.

What we're most curious about now is what people build. If you publish a tool Space, tag it reachy-mini-tool and mcp so others can find it. We'd love to see what Reachy Mini ends up able to do!

Acknowledgements: Many thanks to Fabien Danieau for proofreading this post and helping test the workflow, to Andres Marafioti for helping test it, and to Remi Fabre and the Pollen Robotics team for the ideas and feedback that shaped the remote tools workflow.

MCP Space for Reachy Mini weather briefs.

Great work on making Reachy even easier to customize!How can I add these MCP tools on a wireless Reachy Mini with a preinstalled conversation app?

The tools.txt approach makes the MCP integration especially clear. I like how remote tools are kept separate from the built-in robot tools while still being enabled per profile. The distinction between installing a Space and actually activating its tool IDs in tools.txt also seems important, particularly when multiple remote tools are being used together.I’m also using an MCP server on my site, https://tinid.ph/, to work with AI agents, and it has been really useful for me. In particular, it has helped a lot with identifying and fixing technical issues on the site. The idea of keeping tools accessible to AI agents through MCP, rather than building every capability directly into the application, makes a lot of sense.

#10147. Google Play wants Android apps to nail foldable basics by April 2027

Google Play is introducing new adaptive app and game quality requirements next year to elevate the Android foldable experience.

Starting April 2027, the Play Store will require developers to meet Tier 3 of the Android adaptive app quality guidelines for foldables.

Referred to as “Adaptive ready” or “basic” support, Tier 3 requires apps not to use letterboxing (or other compatibility modes) and to fill the entire screen. During rotation, resizing, and folding/unfolding, apps must preserve scroll position, text input, and media playback. Apps must also support multi-window environments.

Apps that do not meet this quality bar will no longer be able to publish or update on Google Play, and may have reduced visibility on the store.

At the same time, Google Play will require foldable device screenshots for app listings: “Providing foldable screenshots by April 2027 will become a standard submission requirement when publishing new apps or updating your store listing.”

Good. Too many apps aren't foldable ready yet, and that's holding back foldables from adoption in some cases. I hope this year Google really brings their A-game to the Pixel Fold. I really want a foldable.

By August 2027, new and updated apps will be required to target Android 17 (API level 37).

Over time, this “quality framework will progressively expand to incorporate Tier 2 and Tier 1 standards across foldables, tablets, Googlebooks, and Android XR.”

Apps that meet Tier 2 (better) or Tier 1 (best) will get “premier store badging, editorial spotlighting, and enhanced merchandising across Google Play as the platform bar elevates.”

On the gaming front, titles will need to add foldable screenshots to listings by April 2027, while Tier 3 large screen quality guidelines go into effect in August 2027.
